body: 1042 v2 Node to node start up time Version history:(2):Purpose: To reduce system start up time.Source: DPR-LVDS-NETWORK-005:Req10v1,[LVDS_GMSL:2]Verification Method: DemonstrationLegacy ID: 345420v1It is not allowed to have a start-up time of more than 64 ms from system power-on until link is established. To enable full video streaming, no more than another thirteen (13) video frames (corresponding to 433 ms at 30 fps) shall be allowed.Implementation: AllQualification method: Demonstration.4.3.7.4.4 Qualifications MethodsEvery requirement in this document shall be verified according to at least one established qualification method. The method to be used is stated in each requirement at the label “Qualification method”. The most common methods are explained below.Analysis: (Documentation)Documentation showing compliance to the stated requirements. For example datasheets, drawings, reports, pictures etc. which clearly describe how the requirements are met.Test + Analysis: (Documentation of test result)Documentation proving compliance to the stated requirements. Tests shall be performed to verify the compliance, and the tests shall be included in a test plan. The test method and test result shall be presented in a test report. The report shall contain equipment and scenarios used during the test. It shall be possible to trace the requirements in the test document.Demonstration:Compliance to requirements are shown by demonstrating appearance, properties and functionality. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 4.3.7.4.5 Definitions and Abbreviations Definition Description LVDS Low-Voltage Differential Signaling. This term is used in the present document in a wider sense, which is to say that it includes several technologies which utilize a differential signaling scheme with a low-voltage swing; such as Current-Mode Logic (CML, ±800mV), Low-Voltage Positive-Emitter-Coupled Logic (LVPECL, ±800mV), B-LVDS (Bus-LVDS, ±550mV), GMSL (Gigabit Multimedia Serial Link, ±350mV), LDI (LVDS Display Interface, ±350mV), openLDI (±350mV) as well as “pure LVDS” in its original sense with referral to the TIA/EIA-644 standard (±350mV). Serializer A single shift register that receives the parallel data once per parallel clock, and shifts it out to the higher serial clock rate (Parallel in Serial out). Deserializer A device divides the incoming clock down to the parallel rate. There are two registers connected as a double buffer: one is used to clock in the serial stream, and the other is used to hold the data for the slower, parallel side. 1-wire Referring to communicating over a coaxial cable using Texas Instruments chipset. Source A device which produce a collection of data including text, graphics, images, audio and video. Sink A device which process and present data. Node Electronic Control Module. In this context is a node the same as an ECU. Device In this context a device is the same as an electronic component. Pixel Short for picture element. It represents each point of information in an image and each pixel consists of 24 bit RGB data plus up to 8 bits of metadata. Resolution The number of pixels horizontally and vertically. Edge node An ECU (internal vehicle network node) which is the network node that is exposed towards the external network. The node implements a diagnostic over IP-protocol ( DoIP - ISO13400) and provides diagnostic access to test equipment. The LVDS is a high performance data transfer application for today’s new technology. This technology is based on ANSI/TIA/EIA-644 LVDS interface standard. The LVDS technology with a low-voltage differential signal (up to ±800mV; typically ±250mV to ±450mV for the variants based on the mentioned standard) and fast transition time, allows products to reach from 100 Mbps to over 2.5 Gbps of data rate. In addition, the low-voltage swing reduces power dissipation, along with the advantages of differential transmission, i.e. lower electromagnetic interference (EMI). The LVDS technology could be applied for simple line driver and receiver physical layer interface devices and more complex communication chipsets (serializer and deserializer). The LVDS technology can be used over distances ranging from a few centimeters to 10 meters. Today more and more displays are being fitted into vehicles, including the electronic panel that presents speed, revolutions per minute, vehicle status, etc., and multimedia displays for the rear passengers, who can then watch TV or DVDs. Each display requires a video transmission link. Future vehicles may include various cameras to assist the driver, such as cameras for the GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No394(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU rear-view mirror and wing mirror as well as night-vision cameras. Each camera requires its own video transmission link routed to the display. The number of transmission links in the vehicle is thus growing, which is presenting more and more problems in the transmission of analog signals due to electromagnetic interference. By using LVDS links, video interference is thus minimized.The LVDS network layer software need to be an integrated part of the ECU SW.The LVDS physical interface needs low level drivers, as well as higher level of functional usage of the built in setup and test functions of the LVDS link concept.However to make it possible to upload parameters related to the adoption to the actual used length of the cable connection between the ECUs, upon the LVDS link function is implemented on, the parameter sets must be both possible to tune and optimize but also it must be possible to store the correct settings per LVDS link.As an ECU can have multiple LVDS links, both composed upon one-wire implementation, two-wire implementation and four-wire implementation, the settings need to be specific per ECU type, wire length and LVDS link interface.Care should be taken, not only for the local ECU settings for LVDS link side, but also for remote side LVDS settings – parameter settings in the ECU on the other side of the LVDS link, this is due to the overall LVDS link transfer function characteristics – the LVDS link concept will be defined by Serializer, Tx, side settings, cable length/characteristics and the Deserializer, Rx, side settings. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU system, seeFigure System overview of LVDS network.This example network consists of six nodes:· Infotainment Head Unit, IHU (as gateway).· Center Stack Display, CSD (as sink).· Park Assist Camera, PAC (as source).· Night Vision, NV (as source).· Driver Information Module, DIM (as sink).· Head Up Display, HUD (as sink).Please note that this figure above is a typical example.LVDS systems can be less complex – down to two nodes only, composed upon only one type of connectivity, two-wire/four-wire only or it can as above use different selection of LVDS depending of link performance demands.Note also that embedding of Control channels over the LVDS links can be replaced with dedicated automotive bus communication links, redundant to the LVDS embedded Control channel, but the diagnostics functions must always be implemented either over the LVDS Control Channel or by other network protocols.4.3.7.4.8.2 Logical ViewThe topology for communication links between nodes is point-to-point. Each communication link can handle several video streams simultaneously with multiplexing technology, if required.The main function of the LVDS nodes is to distribute video streams from a source to a sink. Depending on the LVDS sources, the nodes can also transform a video stream from one type to another to adopt the image characteristics. Typical transformations can be selection of one two (or more) video stream from the source, into different LVDS destinations. Other transformations can be resize, reshape or resample the incoming LVDS video into the outgoing LVDS video stream.In case the incoming LVDS video is coded, block coded or simply YCrCb (422/420), the node can transform this into more display friendly video streams, like RGB (444) or YCrCb (444). All transformations of the video streams can add latency – please refer to system level requirements in this specification.When there is demand for a shared HMI between nodes, there is a need for high speed data communication. An integrated Ethernet and video link based upon the four-wire option can be selected which supports 2 video channels and up to 100 Mbps of data.The three solutions for LVDS – one-wire, two-wire and four-wire with Ethernet support.4.3.7.4.8.2.1 One-wiredFigures Logical view of serializer and deserializer for the LVDS 1 wire solution. title: Transport and Network layer
body: 1158 v2 Transport and Network layer Version history:(2):Purpose: Reference the transport/network layer standard.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60148v1The transport/network layer required by this document shall be compliant to [CoFR_4] Road vehicles - Communication on FlexRay - Part 2: Communication layer services, ISO 10681-2, CoFlexRay — Part 2: Communication layer services, with the restrictions/additions as defined by this document.4.3.8.1.1.1 Communication Layer Protocol4.3.8.1.1.1.1 Protocol functionsAll messages shall be transmitted as unacknowledged messages. Acknowledged messages shall be supported but not used. i.e. the sender shall not use and the receiver shall accept the acknowledged messages.All messages shall be transmitted with a known message length. Unknown message length shall not be supported, i.e. any message received with unknown message Length shall be ignored.

title: Unacknowledge messages - used
body: 1159 v2 Unacknowledge messages - used Version history:(2):Purpose: Acknowledgement of a diagnostic request and possible retransmission of a message is performed on UDS application layer level.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60156v1All messages shall be transmitted as unacknowledged messages.

title: Known (ML) Message Length - used
body: 1160 v2 Known (ML) Message Length - used Version history:(2):Purpose: In all diagnostic messages the message length is defined which motivates the use of known message length.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60162v1All messages shall be transmitted with a known message length. title: Unknown (ML) Message Length - not supported
body: 1161 v2 Unknown (ML) Message Length - not supported Version history:(2):Purpose: In all diagnostic messages the message length is defined and there is no need to support unknown message length.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60164v1Unknown message length shall not be supported, i.e. any message received with unknown message length shall be ignored.4.3.8.1.1.1.2 Unsegmented and Segmented TransmissionAn unsegmented message is transmitted if the message length is lower than or equal to MFDS for STF C_PDU. A segmented transmission is performed when the message length is greater than the MFDS for STF C_PDU.In order to enhance transmission performance for segmented messages, dynamic frame length (or dynamic data transfer) is not allowed for C_PDUs STF and CF1/CF2. This means that these C_PDUs shall be filled with message data equaling MFDS.The only exception to this requirement is at the end of a segmented message. The last CF1/CF2 C_PDU may contain message data which equals MFDS -1 when the remaining message data length to be transmitted is greater than MFDS of LF C_PDU and lower than the MFDS of CF1/CF2 C_PDU.

A segmented transmission shall be performed when the message length is greater than the MFDS for STF C_PDU.

title: Dynamic frame length for segmented message
body: 1163 v2 Dynamic frame length for segmented message Version history:(2):Purpose: To define the maximum size of an unsegmented message and the minimum size of a segmented message.Source: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60167v1Dynamic frame length for a segmented message (or dynamic data transfer) is not allowed, see Road vehicles - Communication on FlexRay - Part 2: Communication layer services, ISO 10681-2, CoFlexRay — Part 2: Communication layer services - External publications section 7.3.4.3.8.1.1.1.3 Protocol control information (C_PCI)The following sub-sections detail the valid usage of the FlowControl (FC) parameters.4.3.8.1.1.1.3.1 FlowStatus (FS) parametersAll defined FlowStatus (FS) parameters in [CoFR_4] Road vehicles - Communication on FlexRay - Part 2: Communication layer services, ISO 10681-2 shall be supported but only following shall be used: ContinueToSend, Wait, Abort and Overflow. In programming session, the server may use FC.Wait if it receives a request to be queued in server, when it is processing a previously received request. A gateway ECU may use FC.Wait in any situation and session when it does not have enough buffers available for receiving the complete message.

title: FlowControl Wait usage
body: 1164 v4 FlowControl Wait usage Version history:(4):Purpose: Use FC.Wait to halt message reception in appropriate situations.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 116701v3Non-gateway server:In programming session, the server may use FC.Wait if it receives a request when it is processing a previously received request. title: FlowStatus (FS) parameter
body: 1165 v2 FlowStatus (FS) parameter Version history:(2):Purpose: For robustness reasons and future needs all defined FS shall be supported. If one ECU uses the FS value Acknowledge/Retry, used for acknowledged messages, then the communication within the network should continue without disturbance.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60172v1All defined FlowStatus (FS) parameters in Road vehicles - Communication on FlexRay - Part 2: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Communication layer services, ISO 10681-2, CoFlexRay — Part 2: Communication layer services - External publications shall be supported but only following shall be used: ContinueToSend, Wait, Abort and Overflow. 4.3.8.1.1.1.3.2 Maximum number of FC.Wait frame transmissions (C_WFTmax)The C_WFTmax counter shall be set to 255. Note that if an ECU needs to send consecutive FlowControl (FC) C_PDUs with FlowStatus = Wait, then FC.Wait C_PDU shall be sent with periodicity equaling C_Br according to Road vehicles - Communication on FlexRay - Part 2: Communication layer services, ISO 10681-2.See sections Timing parameters in programming session and Timing parameters in non-programming sessions in this specification for the required FC.Wait transmission period.

title: C_WFTmax
body: 1166 v2 C_WFTmax Version history:(2):Purpose: The WAIT mechanism will aid the following dimensioning use cases:- Down stream: Two queued messages are sent to an ECU and the time from the first request received until the final response sent of the first request.- Up stream: Functional address request with unsuppressed response result in a many responses which may need to wait.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60177v1The C_WFTmax counter shall be set to 255 4.3.8.1.1.1.3.3 Bandwidth Control (BC) parameterThe bandwidth control mechanism shall not be used. Consequently, BC parameter shall be set to zero (0). The control of the transfer capability shall only be done with the BufferSize (BfS) parameter.

title: Bandwidth Control (BC) parameter
body: 1167 v3 Bandwidth Control (BC) parameter Version history:(3):Purpose: BC shall be supported for robustness reasons and for future needs. If one ECU incorrectly uses the BC mechanism then the communication within the network continue without disturbance.No bandwidth control mechanism is required. The control of the transfer capability should be done with the BufferSize (BfS) parameter.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60179v2The bandwidth control mechanism shall be supported but not used. Consequently, BC parameter shall be set to zero (0). Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Note: If the BC parameter not is equal to zero (0) then the sender of the message shall use the bandwidth control mechanism defined inRoad vehicles-Communication on FlexRay-Part 2: Communication layer services,ISO 10681-2,CoFlexRay—Part 2: Communication layer services-External publications.4.3.8.1.1.1.3.4 BufferSize (BfS) parameterThe primary use of the BufferSize shall be to restrict the amount of data the sender transmits with Consecutive Frames, before the receiver authorizes continued message transmission. The sender shall not influence the BfS parameter so that a lower amount of data is transmitted than the given BufferSize from the receiver, except for when the end of the message is reached. In all sessions the receiver of a message shall set BfS parameter so that only one FlowControl is used for a certain number of bytes of the message. If the message is longer than this, the receiver will send a Flow Control after each chunk of bytes of the message.If a message is shorter than this is to be received then it is allowed to adapt BfS to indicate a lower value, but the BfS value must be large enough to receive the complete message with only one FlowControl sent by receiver. Using a smaller value for a shorter message allows for more efficient memory usage, especially for gateway ECU where RAM buffers are shared. The minimum number of bytes per each Flow Control depends on the session and whether it is a request or a response.

title: Buffersize (BfS) parameter - sender influence
body: 1168 v2 Buffersize (BfS) parameter - sender influence Version history:(2):Purpose:The primary use of the BufferSize is to restrict the amount of data that the receiver allows the sender to transmit with ConsecutiveFrames, before the receiver authorizes a new ContinueToSend (CTS) of the transmission.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60181v1The sender shall not influence the BufferSize so that a lower amount of data is transmitted than the given BufferSize, except for when the end of the message is reached.

title: Minimum Buffersize (BfS) in programming session server side
body: 1169 v4 Minimum Buffersize (BfS) in programming session server side Version history:(4):Purpose: To harmonize the maximum messages length on different networks and to reduce gateway buffer size.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60182v3For servers and gateway ECUs:In programming session the receiver of a downstream message must respond with a BfS value such that there are never more than one FC C_PDUs per 4095 bytes of data (including the first FC C_PDU) when buffer resources makes 4095 bytes available.Additional for gateway ECU: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU In programming session, if available RAM buffer is less than the length of the message, then BfS value must be so large that all available RAM buffer is used to receive as much as possible of the message, per each FC C_PDU.If available RAM buffer can hold the complete message, it is mandatory to use the smallest RAM buffer available that can hold the complete message. If the server can receive a complete message of 65535 bytes with only one FC C_PDUs, then BfS parameter shall be set to 0x0000.Note for servers and gateway ECUs:It is important to understand the difference of BfS value and requirements for RAM buffer sizes which may be shared between networks.a. Example: receiving a message with total length of 4095 bytes, FPL parameter is 246 in STF C_PDU. BfS parameter in FC C_PDU must be at least 4095-246=3849 if RAM buffer is available.b. Example: receiving a message with total length of 1000 bytes, FPL parameter is 246 in STF C_PDU. BfS parameter in FC C_PDU must be at least 1000-246=754 if RAM buffer is available.Note for gateway ECU:c. Minimum RAM for request buffers in gateway requirements may require RAM buffer size to be larger than the value implied by the BfS parameter in this requirement.d. Example: Assume FPL parameter is 246 in STF C_PDU. A gateway ECU is required to have total 4kB RAM buffer, it receives a 1kB message A, respond BfS=3849, then 3kB buffer is free. Another message B arrives which is 4kB. The gateway ECU must respond with BfS=3kB-246=2826 initially, and later try to receive the remaining 1kB.

Minimum RAM for request buffers in gateway requirements may require RAM buffer size to be larger than the value implied by the BfS parameter in this requirement.a. Example: receiving a message with total length of 1024 bytes, FPL parameter is 24 in STF C_PDU. BfS parameter in FC C_PDU must be at least 1024-14=1000.b. Example: receiving a message with total length of 200 bytes, FPL parameter is 24 in STF C_PDU. BfS parameter in FC C_PDU must be at least 200-14=176.c. Example: Assume FPL parameter is 24 in STF C_PDU. A gateway ECU is required to have total 4kB RAM buffer, it receives three 1kB messages A, B and C, and responds BfS=1024-24=1000 for all of them, then 1kB buffer is free. Another message D arrives which is 2kB, the gateway must respond with BfS=1kB-24=1000 initially, and later try to receive the remaining 1kB.d. The timeout and performance requirement values can vary between down and up stream messages. 4.3.8.1.1.2.1 Timing parameters in programming sessionWhen the NetworkStatus parameter equals Boot according to [CoFR_2] FlexRay Data Link Layer then table below shall apply. The duration of a FlexRay cycle (gdCycle) is defined in [CoFR_2] FlexRay Data Link Layer. Timing Parameter Description Timeout(ms) Performance requirement(ms) C_As Time for transmission of the FlexRay frame (any C_PDU) on the sender side. Timeout = cycle time * 200 N/A C_Ar Time for transmission of the FlexRay frame (any C_PDU) on the receiver side. Timeout = cycle time * 200 N/A C_Bs Time until reception of the next FlowControl C_PDU. The ECU must not start flashing the TransferDatablock after the complete TransferData block has been received. If the C_Data Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU (transferRequestParameterRecord) is compressed, all C_Data from each C_PDU shall be sent to the layer where decompression is performed, and that layer shall in turn send data as soon as it is decompressed to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions.This contradicts normal specified transport layer behaviour since it states that the transport layer shall only send complete messages to upper layers. This decrease the time it takes to perform TransferData by writing frame by frame to flash memory. The ECU shall be able to write the data while receiving new data and therefore the ECU will not need to write as much data at the last message and thus the P4 time will be shorter leading to shorter SWDL time.

title: Forward C_Data from each C_PDU to upper layer
body: 1197 v2 Forward C_Data from each C_PDU to upper layer Version history:(2):Purpose: Decrease the time it takes to perform TransferData via writing frame by frame.The ECU will be able to write the data while receiving new data and thus the ECU will not need to write as much data at the last message and thus the P4 time will be shorter leading to shorter SWDL time.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 128928v1While a diagnostic server is receiving a segmented request for TransferData 0x36 the transport protocol layer shall send all C_Data from each C_PDU to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions (optional for all other services). If the C_Data is compressed, all C_Data from each C_PDU shall be sent to the layer where decompression is performed, and that layer shall in turn send data as soon as it is decompressed to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions.Note: this contradicts and shall override ISO specified transport layer behaviour which states that the transport layer shall only send complete diagnostic messages to upper layers.Depending on programming alignment constraints of the flash memory, the actual programming may have to be aligned according to the flash memory and not immediately when data bytes are available from transport layer or decompression layer.Example 1: Uncompressed C_Data, length of L_PDU is 254 bytes, C_Data is 246 bytes; a microcontroller has capability to write only 4 bytes at a time into program memory, e.i. not 2 bytes in one event and adjacent 2 bytes in another event. In this case the flash programming function has to reassemble groups of 4 bytes for programming, and must queue any received bytes less than 4 until further bytes are received to get at a group of 4 bytes. In this case 61 * 4 = 244 bytes of the 246 bytes C_Data from STF can be programmed immediately by upper layer, and 2 bytes (246-244) queued and joined with first 2 bytes from the first CF and so on. If the length of the C_Data to be programmed is such that at the end, a group of 4 bytes can not be made, the reaining bytes, less than 4, are forwarded to upper layer anyway.Example 2: Uncompressed C_Data, length of L_PDU is 254 bytes, C_Data is 246 bytes; a microcontroller has capability to write only 256 bytes at a time time into program memory. In this case the flash programming function has to reassemble groups of 256 bytes for programming, and must queue any received bytes less than 256. In this case 246 bytes C_Data in STF and 10 bytes C_Data in first CF for a total of 256 bytes will be received until flash programming can start when the beginning of TransferData request is received. After that, 236 bytes (246-10) will be queued and reassembled with 20 bytes of the following CF until 256 new bytes are received. If the length of the C_Data to be programmed is such that at the end, a group of 4 bytes can not be made, the reaining bytes, less than 256, are forwarded to Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU upper layer anyway.4.3.8.1.1.5 Frame payload length, normal application schedule 1The maximum frame size of the diagnostic request or response messages shall be selected such that segmentation of a message is avoided. Segmentation of response messages will not be possible to avoid in all situations, e.g. DRO responses containing composite DIDs.The sender of a message shall dynamically resize the frame payload length if the message is shorter than the maximum defined payload.The unused data bytes of a FlexRay frame shall be padded with zero (0x00). An ECU shall not reject a received FlexRay frame with non-zero pad bytes, however.

Furthermore, this specification is applicable for both FlexRay Schedule Coordinator Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU and FlexRay ECUs according to Figure below .All diagnostic messages on FlexRay shall be sent and received according to the documents referenced in section Requisite documents and this specification. Geely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd 005 01 426(1572 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU static segment a static time division multiple access scheme is used to arbitrate transmissions. Within the dynamic segment a dynamic mini-slotting based scheme is used to arbitrate transmissions. The symbol window is a communication period in which a symbol can be transmitted.The network idle time is a communication-free period that concludes each cycle. cycle time The time duration of a cycle. FlexRay ECU A FlexRay ECU that is present within the FlexRay network and not is responsible to coordinate the active schedule FlexRay Schedule Coordinator A FlexRay ECU that is responsible to coordinate which schedule that shall be present on its network, only one FlexRay Schedule Coordinator can be present within a FlexRay network. MFDS, Maximum Frame Data Size The maximum frame data size denotes maximum data length of C_Data for a C_PDU. The length of C_Data will vary between CF1/CF2/CFEOB and STF/LF C_PDUs. C_Data maximum data length will vary for up and down stream messages. N/A Not applicable NetworkStatus parameter Defines which FlexRay schedule is presently active. Non-programming sessions Any diagnostic session other than programming session. Server side The side of an ECU which sends a diagnostic response on the specific network. The ECU may either be a server or a gateway transferring a diagnostic response from a lower level network. Tester A system that controls functions such as test, inspection, monitoring, or diagnosis of an on-vehicle electronic control unit and may be dedicated to a specific type of operators (e.g. a scan tool dedicated to garage mechanics or a test tool dedicated to assembly plant agents). The tester is also referenced as the client. Up stream Diagnostic message communication in the direction from server to client is regarded as an up stream communication. title: Supporting functional requests
body: 1229 v2 Supporting functional requests Version history:(2):Purpose: Define support for functional requests.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60112v1Functional requests shall be supported.4.3.9.1.1.2 CAN frame data paddingFor Classic CAN the DLC (Data Length Code) contained in every CAN frame shall always be set to eight. Any CAN frame with a DLC different from eight shall be considered invalidly formatted and ignored by the recipient.For CAN FD the DLC (Data Length Code) contained in every CAN frame shall always be set to a value within the range 8 to 15. Any CAN frame with a DLC outside this range shall be considered invalidly formatted and ignored by the recipient.Unused data shall be padded with 0x00 and the receiver of the frame shall not check the padding.NoteThe number of bytes in the data field of a CAN frame shall be indicated by the DLC. This DLC shall consist of 4 bits. The admissible number of data bytes for Classic CAN frames shall range from 0 to 8. DLCs in the range of 0 to 7 shall indicate data fields of length of 0 to 7 bytes. In Classical CAN frames, all other DLCs shall indicate that the data field is 8 bytes long. In CAN FD frames, DLCs in the range of 0 to 8 shall indicate data fields of length 0 to 8 bytes, while the other DLCs code longer data fields, according to the table below (see [DoCAN_3] ISO 11898- Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 1). body: 1231 v3 Handling of CAN requests in regards of DLC Version history:(3):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 60130v1USDT request frames with a DLC not equal to eight (8) for Classic CAN, or outside the range 8-15 for CAN FD, shall be considered invalidly formatted and be ignored by the recipient.

title: Unused data in the CAN frame
body: 1232 v2 Unused data in the CAN frame Version history:(2):Purpose: Define what to do with data not used in the USDT frame.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60133v1Unused data shall be padded with 0x00 and the receiver of the frame shall ignore padding.4.3.9.1.1.3 Use data frame by frameWhile receiving a segmented request for TransferData 0x36 the transport protocol shall send all N_Data from each N_PDU immediately to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions (optional for all other services). The ECU must not start flashing the TransferData block after the complete TrasferData block has been received. If the N_Data (transferRequestParameterRecord) is compressed, all N_Data from each N_PDU shall be sent to the layer where decompression is performed, and that layer shall in turn send data as soon as it is decompressed to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions.This contradicts normal specified transport layer behaviour since it states that the transport layer shall only send complete messages to upper layers. This decrease the time it takes to perform TransferData by writing frame by frame to flash memory. The ECU shall be able to write the data while receiving new data and therefore the ECU will not need to write as much data at the last message and thus the P4 time will be shorter leading to shorter SWDL time.

title: Forward N_Data from each N_PDU to upper layer
body: 1233 v2 Forward N_Data from each N_PDU to upper layer Version history:(2):Purpose: Decrease the time it takes to perform TransferData via writing frame by frame.The ECU will be able to write the data while receiving new data and thus the ECU will not need to write as much data at the last message and thus the P4 time will be shorter leading to shorter SWDL time.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 128908v1 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU While a diagnosotic server is receiving a segmented request for TransferData 0x36 the transport protocol layer shall send all N_Data from each N_PDU to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions (optional for all other services). If the N_Data is compressed, all N_Data from each N_PDU shall be sent to the layer where decompression is performed, and that layer shall in turn send data as soon as it is decompressed to upper layers that contain the flash programming functions.Note: this contradicts and shall override ISO specified transport layer behaviour which states that the transport layer shall only send complete diagnostic messages to upper layers.Depending on programming alignment constrains of the flash memory, the actual programming of bytes may have to be aligned according to the flash memory and not performed immediately when data bytes are available from transport layer or decompression layer.Example 1: Uncompressed N_Data; a microcontroller has capability to write only 4 bytes at a time into program memory, e.i. not 2 bytes in one event and adjacent 2 bytes in another event.In this case the flash programming function has to reassemble groups of 4 bytes for programming, and must queue any received bytes less than 4 until further bytes are received to get at a group of 4 bytes. In this case 4 bytes of the 6 bytes N_Data from FirstFrame can be programmed immediately, and 2 bytes (6-4) queued and joined with first 2 bytes from the first Consecutive Frame and so on. If the length of the data to be programmed is such that at the end, a group of 4 bytes can not be made, the reaining bytes, less than 4, are written anyway.Example 2: Uncompressed N_Data; a microcontroller has capability to write only 256 bytes at a time time into program memory. In this case the flash programming function has to reassemble groups of 256 bytes for programming, and must queue any received bytes less than 256. In this case FirstFrame + 36 Consecutive Frames (7 bytes N_Data in FF and 252 bytes N_Data in 36 CF:s for a total of 259 bytes) will be received until flash programming can start when the beginning of TransferData request is received, and 3 bytes (259-256) will be queued and reassembled with the following Consecutive Frames until at least 256 new bytes are received. If the length of the data to be programmed is such that at the end, a group of 256 bytes can not be made, the reaining bytes, less than 256, are written anyway. Bytes are queued and aligned until sets of 4 bytes can be forwarded to the upper layer for immediate programming. The ECU can flash memory at least at the same speed as data from Consecutive Frames are received. Note: Example A is for Classic CAN (DLC = 8) or CAN FD where DLCs above 8 are not used. A CAN FD example with DLCs above 8 would still require that bytes are queued and aligned for the last fraction of the 4 bytes set in every Consecutive Frame. However, more sets of 4 bytes can immediately be programmed for every Consecutive Frame due to that the DLC is above 8. Bytes are aligned in sets of 4 bytes and forwarded to the upper layer for queued programming. The ECU can not flash memory at the same speed as data from Consecutive Frames are received. Note: Example B is for Classic CAN (DLC = 8) or CAN FD where DLCs above 8 are not used. A CAN FD example with DLCs above 8 would still require that bytes are queued and aligned for the last fraction of the 4 bytes set in every Consecutive Frame. More sets of 4 bytes sets in every Consecutive Frame imply that more data per Consecutive Frame will be forwarded to the upper layer for queued programming. ## 4.3.9.1.2 Transport layer protocol The transport/network layer required by this document shall be compliant to [DoCAN\_2] Road vehicles – Diagnostic communication over Controller Area Network (DoCAN) - Part 2: Transport protocol and network layer services, with the restrictions/additions as defined by the subsequent sub-sections. This document specifies OEM specific requirements. If there are other kinds or requirements like legislative requirements (for example OBD requirements), these requirements may have higher priority than the requirements in this specicifation. However if the other requirements have performance requirements lower than the performance requirements specified in this document, the performance requirements in this document shall be followed. This is valid as long as the performance requirement in this document does not contradict timeout GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No434(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU requirements in the other document.

title: Precedence of requirements
body: 1199 v2 Precedence of requirements Version history:(2):Purpose: Define which set of requirements to use for which circumstances.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 60004v1 If there are other kinds or requirements like legislative requirements (for example OBD requirements), these requirements may have higher priority than the requirements in this specification. However if the other requirements have performance requirements lower than the performance requirements specified in this document, the performance requirements in this document shall be followed. This is valid as long as the performance requirement in this document does not contradict timeout requirements in the other document. 4.3.9.1.2.1 Protocol control information specification 4.3.9.1.2.1.1 BlockSize (BS) parameter definitionWhen in a non-programming session, both the server and client side shall be able to receive a complete diagnostic message without sending any intermediate flow control frames, to ensure as swift communication as possible. Client side shall be able to receive 4095 bytes diagnostic message without sending any flow control frames i.e. BlockSize = 0x00.Block size for CAN using 8 bytes frame length Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU When in a non-programming session the server shall be able to receive diagnostic messages of at least 100 bytes without sending flow control frames. Translated into block size the server shall be able to receive 100/(7 bytes / CF), which rounds up to 15 Consecutive Frames, i.e. the server shall have a BlockSize parameter set to 15 (0x0F) or larger, e.i. BlockSize 1 to 14 is not allowed. Server may also set BlockSize to 0x00 if it is capable of receiving 4095 bytes diagnostic message without sending Flow Control frames.Block size for CAN FD using 64 byte frame lengthWhen in a non-programming session the server shall be able to receive diagnostic messages of at least 200 bytes without sending flow control frames. Translated into block size the server shall be able to receive 300/(64 bytes / CF), which rounds up to 5 Consecutive Frames, i.e. the server shall have a BlockSize parameter set to 5 (0x05) or larger, e.i. BlockSize 1 to 4 is not allowed. Server may also set BlockSize to 0x00 if it is capable of receiving 4095 bytes diagnostic message without sending Flow Control frames.When in programming session server side shall be able to receive a complete diagnostic message of 4095 bytes without sending any intermediate Flow Control frames i.e. BlockSize shall always be 0x00 for all services the server supports.

title: BlockSize parameter non-programming session client side
body: 1201 v3BlockSize parameter non-programming session client side Version history:(3):Purpose:Define BlockSize for non-programming session client side. For more information see section BlockSize (BS) parameter definition. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60007v2For ECU gatewaying responses from CAN to another network:In non-programming session the receiver of an upstream message must respond with BS=0 so that there are never more than one FlowControl N_PDUs per 4095 bytes of data (including the first FlowControl N_PDU) when buffer resources makes 4095 bytes available.In non-programming session, if the largest available RAM buffer is less than the length of the message, that buffer must be used, and BS set so that all of that buffer is used. This will reduce the number of FlowControl N_PDU used for reception of the complete message.It is mandatory to use the smallest RAM buffer available that can hold the complete message, when such buffer is available.Note:Example A: A 300 bytes message is received, and the only RAM buffer available is 4095 bytes.BS is 0 or at least 42.Example B: A 300 bytes message is received, and RAM buffers are available with 50 bytes and 100 bytes, so none of the buffers can hold the complete message. A 100 bytes RAM buffer is used in favour of 50 bytes buffers, which reduce the number of FlowControl N_PDUs. BS will be 13.

title: BlockSize parameter programming session client side

For more information see section BlockSize (BS) parameter definition.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60009v1BlockSize (BS) shall always be 0x00 in programming session for client side4.3.9.1.2.1.2 Separation (STmin) parameter definitionThe STmin parameter shall reflect the maximum processing time the ECU needs to have in between each CAN frame, regardless of ECU state or activity. For example if an ECU sets a STmin time of 1ms, the supplier must guarantee that the ECU is always able to process Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU consecutive frames at this rate. Preferably the STmin time shall be as low as possible, but the server is allowed to set a maximum of 15ms. Client side shall be dimensioned to handle STmin time of 0 which means CAN frames are being sent back to back. The reason why STmin requirement is tougher for gateways than the ECU's on the network is:When in non-programming session, most requests requiring some performance are small enough to be fitted into one frame.More lenient requirements lessen the burden on the servers, making it possible to use ECU's with less performance as servers.When in programming session both server and client side shall be able to handle receiving frames with no separation time primarily for 2 purposes.Considering the amount of data to transfer via diagnostics when in programming session compared to the other sessions, the need for speed is greater when in programming session.Since when in bootloader mode the ECU will not be burden by simultaneously running the normal functionality supported by the ECU, the ECU shall be able to handle this extra processor load.

This applies regardless of whether the single frames are received from one or more servers.Examples for a server:a: queued request where both the first and second request each fits in a single frame.Examples for a gateway ECU:b: a server sends negative response NRC 0x78 and immediately after it sends final response.c: several servers sends negative response NRC 0x78 and immediately after they send final responses.In these examples and if using 500kbps bit rate up to four single frames shall be received within one millisecond.

This applies both when the single frames are Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU from the same sender and from different senders.Note: the shortest separation time of CAN frames is the minimum Interframe Space.4.3.9.1.2.2 Maximum number of FC. Wait frame transmission (N_WFTmax)The N_WFTmax counter shall be set to 255 (0xFF). In programming session, the server may use FC.Wait if it receives a request to be queued in server, when it is processing a previously received request. A gateway ECU may use FC.Wait in any situation and session when it does not have enough buffers available for receiving the complete message.

title: Flowcontrol Wait usage
body: 1211 v3 Flowcontrol Wait usage Version history:(3):Purpose: Use FC.Wait to halt message reception in appropriate situations.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 115798v2Non-gateway server:In programming session, the server may use FC.Wait if it receives a request when it is Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU processing a previously received request. In all other situations in all sessions usage of FC.Wait is not allowed.Gateway ECU:The gateway ECU shall use FC.Wait if it receives a message when buffers are not available for receiving the complete message. This applies to server side and client side.4.3.9.1.2.3 Network layer timing4.3.9.1.2.3.1 Timing parametersThe time it takes to send one CAN frame (N_Ar and N_As) depends on the bit rate of the CAN network and if the bit rate is set to 500kbit/s the lowest possible value for N_Ar and N_As is 250 μs. If a CAN with a different bit rate is used, performance of N_Ar and N_As will have to be recalculated.Different parameter values applies depending on if the ECU is in programming or non-programming session.The network layer timing parameters for non-programming session is described in Table - Timing parameters non-programming session. Item Parameter Timeout value Performance requirement value 1 N_As 1000 ms - 2 N_Ar 1000 ms - 3 N_Bs 1000 ms - 4 N_Br - N_Br < 20 ms for FC.CTS and FC.OVFLW.For FC.Wait the periodicity shall be N_Bs * 0.9 = 900ms ± 50ms. 5 N_Cs - N_Cs < 20 ms. 6 N_Cr 1000ms - Table - Timing parameters non-programming session The network layer timing parameters for programming session is described in Table - Timing parameters programming session. Item Parameter Timeout value Performance requirement value 1 N_As 1000 ms - 2 N_Ar 1000 ms - 3 N_Bs 1000 ms - 4 N_Br N_Br < 2000 μs for FC.CTS and FC.OVFLW.For FC.WT the periodicity shall be N_Bs * 0.9 = 900ms ± 50ms. 5 N_Cs N_Cs < 100 μs 6 N_Cr 1000 ms - Table - Timing parameters programming session All requirements from this section are specified in section Requirements from section Timing parameters.Note: When performance timing is verified, timestamp information normally shows time at start of each frame. In such case it is important to know that N_Ar/N_As is included when e.g. evaluating N_Br and N_Cs performance. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU

title: N_Br Performance requirement in non-programming session for FC.CTS andFC.OVFLW
body: 1215 v4 N_Br Performance requirement in non-programming session for FC.CTS andFC.OVFLW Version history:(4):Purpose: The time spent waiting shall be minimized. Although N_Br time does not affect the transmission time as much as N_Cs time, the diagnostic kernel scheduling Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU shall still be done with the same frequencySource: Table - Timing parameters non-programming session, item 4Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60062v3N_Br shall be N_Br < 20 ms for FC.CTS and FC.OVFLW when in non-programming session.Note:a. If other CAN frames with higher priority exist on CAN, then a FC N_PDU may be delayed due to CAN protocol arbitration. The requirement is applicable and verifiable only when no such frame exist.b. For a client side of a gateway sending parallel requests, the CAN frames will have different CAN identifiers and hence different priority, and actual N_Cs may be higher than the requirement, this is expected.c. For a server, if other servers are sending responses in parallel then a FC N_PDU may be delayed due to CAN protocol arbitration, this is expected.d. The Autosar CAN Transport Layer configuration parameter CanTpNbr is not configuring the N_Br performance for the first transmitted FlowControl after a FirstFrame although CanTpNbr is stated to be a performance configuration parameter. Instead CanTpNbr is configuring an internal timeout of getting internal buffer resources for use in subsequent reception of Consecutive Frames and affect the time between a previous FlowControl and a subsequent FlowControl.

body: 1216 v5 N_Br Performance requirement in non-programming session for FC.Wait Version history:(5):Purpose: The time that an ECU may wait before sending a FC.Wait frame must be lower than the specified timeout to ensure the sending ECU does not time out the message. To prevent unnecessary bus load and minimize the risk that N_WFTmax counter is overrun, the periodicity of the FC.Wait frame shall be as high as possible.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60063v4FC.Wait frames shall be sent with a periodicity of N_Cr * 0.9 = 900ms ± 50ms non-programming session.Note:a. If other CAN frames with higher priority exist on CAN, then a FC N_PDU may be delayed due to CAN protocol arbitration. The requirement is applicable and verifiable only when no such frame exist.b. For a client side of a gateway sending parallel requests, the CAN frames will have different CAN identifiers and hence different priority, and actual N_Cs may be higher than the requirement, this is expected.c. For a server, if other servers are sending responsesin parallel then a FC N_PDU may be delayed due to CAN protocol arbitration, this is expected.d. The Autosar CAN Transport Layer configuration parameter CanTpNbr is not configuring the N_Br performance for the first transmitted FlowControl after a FirstFrame although CanTpNbr is stated to be a performance configuration parameter. Instead CanTpNbr is configuring an internal timeout of getting internal buffer resources for use in subsequent reception of Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Consecutive Frames and affect the time between a previous FlowControl and a subsequent FlowControl.

title: N_Cs Performance requirement in non-programming session
body: 1217 v5 N_Cs Performance requirement in non-programming session Version history:(5):Purpose: The time spent waiting shall be minimized and especially for N_Cs since N_Cs wait time is the factor that affects the transfer rates the most. If the send mechanism is performed in application schedule context (compared to sending on Tx interrupt), the ECU needs to poll the send function more often, and thus less time will be spent on the applications normal functionality.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 60064v4When in non-programming session, the ECU shall be able to send Consecutive Frames with N_Cs less than 20ms.Note:a. If other CAN frames with higher priority exist on CAN, then a FC N_PDU may be delayed due to CAN protocol arbitration. The requirement is applicable and verifiable only when no such frame exist.b. For a client side of a gateway sending parallel requests, the CAN frames will have different CAN identifiers and hence different priority, and actual N_Cs may be higher than the requirement, this is expected.c. For a server, if other servers are sending responses in parallel then a FC N_PDU may be delayed due to CAN protocol arbitration, this is expected.d. The Autosar CAN Transport Layer configuration parameter CanTpNcs is not configuring the N_Cs performance defined by ISO-15765 although it is stated to be a performance configuration parameter. Instead CanTpNcs is configuring an internal timeout of getting data to be placed in the next Consecutive Frame. I.e. if no data can be retrieved internally for sending in a new Consecutive Frame, the sender will abort the transmission after CanTpNcs elapsed.

ISO specifications VCC specifications (relation to ISO) OSI Layer 7 Application OSI Layer 6 Presentation OSI Layer 5 Session OSI Layer 4 Transport OSI Layer 3 Network OSI Layer 2 Data Link OSI Layer 1 Physical GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No449(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 4.3.10 DoIP Communication4.3.10.1 DoIP - Generic Info4.3.10.1.1 IntroductionDiagnostic communication Over IP (DoIP) is a standard developed by ISO for vehicle communication over the Internet Protocol (IP). It introduces a session layer protocol in the OSI model (see diagram in chapter Overview) for sending and receiving data over.This document will for the most part provide specifications regarding optional features in the DoIP standard.It will also specify hard limits for some "open" values and specify a variety of manufacturer specific values.It will have two Chapters: One for specifying the DoIP requirements for the ECU called "Edge Node".This is the only DoIP ECU in the vehicle.The other Chapter contains requirements for how to handle DoIP communication with the remaining IP ECUs in the vehicle network.The document shall be seen as a companion to the official DoIP specification, giving directions on how we expect the DoIP protocol to behave. This document always has higher precedence over ISO-13400 documents and for conflicting information, this document shall be valid.Anyone who implements the Edge Node, IP ECUs or Tester equipment that shall communicate with these ECUs should read this document. It can also be used as a starting point for testers.The DoIP standard is very open-ended regarding its network design. A vehicle can e.g. expose several DoIP ECUs to the outside world, individually or organized in groups and so forth.The main idea in the vehicle network is to expose a single DoIP ECU and to provide only one IP address to the tester. This makes things like GID synchronization superfluous. The only ECU exposed to a tester is called the Edge Node and all DoIP communication with the vehicle will pass through this ECU. This gives several advantages. With only one point of information flow into the vehicle, one can implement several security mechanisms, which are normally associated with firewalls and intrusion detection systems in "normal" computer network systems. Another advantage with this design is conservation of IP-addresses. There is no ambiguity regarding the mapping between vehicle and IP-addresses. The routing of DoIP messages and diagnostic traffic is also generalized in the Edge Node, e.g. some packets are destined for a Flexray network and some are destined for an internal Ethernet network. For further information regarding routing and gateways please see [IP Routing] and [Diagnostic and Bootloader Gateway Specification].4.3.10.1.1.1 Definitions & Abbreviations Abbr. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure: Reception of a signal in an asynchronous systemExplanations to the numbers in the Figure: Reception of a signal in an asynchronous system and description of the execution flow:1. The signal is received through the CAN interface. The message is transferred unprocessed to the application (A) SW.2. The same unprocessed message as in 1 is also supplied to the monitor (M) SW.3. The signal is used as input to (A). This SW has to include the different error detection mechanisms, and also transient filters on the error reactions.4. Application (A) will generate some kind of function output, which will be used both to control the actual output (e.g. digital out, CAN-message) and as input to (M).5. (M) will use the signal and the application function output and apply some application specific plausibility check(s). Those checks are described in the SWRS for the ECU.6. In case (M) detects error in the plausibility check it will be able to inhibit the output from (A). The specific mechanism is also application dependant, but shall ensure that a faulty application SW should not be able to cause a hazardous situation. The mechanism is described in the SWRS for the ECU.7. In order to fulfill the requirements (A) and (M) must perform mutual monitoring of the other's error detection capabilities, i.e. (M) must check that (A) detects error(s) correctly and (A) must check that (M) detects error(s) correctly.4.3.11.1.2 Appendix C - Transient FilterA transient filter is necessary to be tolerant to a number of transient failures in the received data. The filter will also make it possible to require a number of correct messages before the received data is regarded as correct. Such a transient filter can be implemented with a counter. If errors are detected in the received data, the counter is incremented and if correct data is received the counter is decremented.The counter has programmable counting factors so that the time until a transient fault is regarded permanent and the time from when the error disappears until it is regarded fault free can be individually adjustable. At a certain level of the error counter the error is regarded permanent and failure management actions are taken. The counting stops at a certain level in order to limit recovery time. When the counter has returned to zero it is assumed that the fault has disappeared. The different limits shall be possible to calibrate from zero to 255. The counting factors shall be possible to calibrate from 1 to 10. This principle is described in Figure: Principle for the transient filter, "permanent error" for permanent errors and in Figure: Principle for the transient filter, "intermittent error" for intermittent errors Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU Error detection Transient counter Counter increase value Transient filtered error time Counter stop limit Counter error limit Counter decrease value time time Figure: Principle for the transient filter, "permanent error". Error detection Transient counter Counter stop limit Counter error limit Counter decrease value Transient filtered error time time Figure: Principle for the transient filter, "intermittent error". NOTE: When an incorrect signal is received, a replacement value for the Data usually has to be used temporarily by the application (e.g. the last received correct Data is used until a correct signal is received). ```txt GEELY Geely Automotive Research Institute (Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document Type Note-SWRS Document No Revision 005 Document Release Status RELEASED Revision Volume No 01 Page No 457(1572) Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU 4.3.11.1.3 Appendix D - Handling of Difference in Generation and Consumption Rates Depending upon the practical situation of the relationship between the signal generation frequency and the consumption frequency, we get three (3) different cases: 1. The consumption of the signal is done at a rate which is at least the rate of the generation. This is the ideal case and will allow the receiver to check that all values of the U-Cnt are monotonically increasing (disregarding the U-Cnt wrap-around) and thus provide the strongest error checking capability. 2. The consumption of the signal is done at the same rate as the rate of the generation. In this case the receiving ECU has to take into account the jitter between the producing ECU and itself. The value of U-Cnt may not be updated when expected (no new signal has been received) as well as U-Cnt value might step over one value (one signal has been missed). This is no optimal case, and this has to be taken into account in the receiving node (e.g. in the calibration of the transient filters or in special SW). 3. The consumption of the signal is done at a rate which is slower than the rate of the generation. In this case the receiving ECU has to take into account not only the jitter between the producing ECU and itself, but also the higher production rate. Individual signal will for sure be missed, and U-Cnt values might step over several values. This has to be taken into account in similar ways as in (2) above. The following algorithm can be used to handle the situation described in (2) above: u_cnt_sum += u_cnt - u_cnt_old - 1; u_cnt_old = u_cnt; if ((u_cnt_sum > 1) || (u_cnt_sum = FC_FAULTLIMIT) { error = true; } else if (fault_cnt == 0) { error = false; } 4.3.11.1.4 Appendix E - Proposal for Distributed Run-Time Fault Injection Design details regarding the run-time fault injection can vary from implementations but one approach could include the following steps (assuming the transmitting and receiving node are both asynchronous double CPU systems): Transmitting node 1 time out of N, the application SW should generate an erroneous signal that intentionally triggers the monitor to inhibit the sending of this particular signal. (This will typically be twice per minute (ap-proximately 100 times per hour) to minimize the risk for undiscovered errors and compensate for the fact that the transmitting and receiving nodes are not synchronized.) In the asynchronous system this will include the switching between Application generating Data error (in which case the signal shall be blocked by a correctly working monitor and resulting in that the receiving node will detect a counter error) and the generation of incorrect checksum ``` GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Note-SWRS RELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No458(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU values (in which case a correctly working receiving node shall detect the checksum error).Receiving nodeThe error reaction (inhibit of application output by the monitor) should be checked at least once every driving cycle (during initialization or shut-down, if not possible during normal operation). Based upon the knowledge that the transmitting node will generate erroneous signals 1 times out of N, an additional error detection mechanism should take this into account. The failure to detect any errors for a certain time (matched against the figure N) is also to be treated as an error.NOTE: By having the transmitting node performing the run-time fault injection the total need for implementation of run-time fault injection routines will be kept to a minimum. Furthermore the necessity for robustness against transient errors in the receiving ECUs will be visible early in the development phase.4.3.11.1.5 Appendix F - Example of Transmission Manager on Sender ECU Scenario:Data is calculated by SW-C 1 and transferred as dataEI1 to SW-C 3 (ASIL C transmission manager).SW-C 3 performs a sanity check of ASIL C properties of dataEI1.If sanity check shows that ASIL C properties are fulfilled, E2E library is called with dataEI1 as parameter (E2E_Protect(&dataEI1...))If sanity check shows that ASIL C properties are not fulfilled, E2E library is called with safe state of dataEI1 as parameter (E2E_Protect(&safetstatedataEI1...)) Signal is transferred to RTE as follows: signal 1 = CRC from E2E, signal 2=counter from E2E, signal 3=dataEI1.SW-C 3 and E2E lib is implemented in ASIL C part of software. Freedom of interference between partitions SW-C 1 and SW-C 3 according to ISO26262 has to be fulfilled.Note:signal3 is equal to dataEI1 even if sanity check in SW-C 3 detects that ASIL C properties are not fulfilled. This is due to that SW-C 1 shall always set dataEI1 to safestate in case ASIL C properties are not fulfilled.This means that CRC will be correct as long as SW-C 1 is calculating data correct with respect to ASIL C properties. If SW-C 1 does not calculate ASIL C properties correctly CRC will be corrupt.Note:SW-C 2 and dataEI2 is not used in this example.4.3.11.1.6 Appendix A - Examples of Monitored Signal GenerationIt is assumed that a signal is produced by an ECU with two independent HW components (e.g. CPUs) sharing one CAN interface. The SW generating the signal can be arranged logically in four (4) different com-positions. Those are illustrated in Figure:The four (4) different logical compositions for the SW generating signals and described according to the following (note that the descriptions are simplified, and some details have been left out):1. The application (A) is responsible for generation of the signal contents, and for the sending of the signal on the bus. The application monitor (M) is responsible for checking that the Data part of the signal is ok, otherwise (M) shall prevent (A) from sending this signal on the bus.2. The application (A) is responsible for generation of the signal contents. The application monitor (M) is responsible for checking that the Data part of the signal is ok, and for the sending of the signal on the bus. If (M) detects an error in the Data part of the signal, the sending of this signal shall be blocked.3. The same case as in (1) above, but with a monitor (m) that monitors the application monitor (M). By having (m) performing run-time fault injection into (M), the correct operation of (M) is ensured. This lay-out is necessary when (A) and (M) runs within the same CPU without HW redundancy.4. Similar to case (3) above. The difference is that the application monitor (M) is responsible for the sending of the signal on the CAN-bus. The guideline consists of two parts. The first part is a guide to be used when selecting suitable safety mechanisms depending on failure modes to be handled and their ASIL. The second part includes a list of suitable safety mechanisms for system signaling with the related failure modes.The appendix in the document provides a set of safety mechanisms, patterns and examples that relates to different aspects of distributed functionality and safety related communication.4.3.11.1.7.2 MotivationThis guideline exists to provide guidance and harmonize the use of safety mechanisms in network communication. The guideline is also a part of ISO-26262 compliance for functions, systems, and components. It shall be demonstrated that the selected safety mechanisms provide sufficient fault handling capabilities for the considered network.The recommendations in this guideline are based on the recommendations in [SafeCom_1] for communication using E2E that are developed by safety experts within AUTOSAR for up to ASIL D communication. These recommendations shall be confirmed to be appropriate in the Item, fulfilling the Item's own safety requirements and any external safety requirements. These additional safety mechanisms are intended to protect against faults occurring in the communication stack and also to enhance protection against faults occurring on the communication bus itself. It is a packet oriented system with mechanisms for flow control, data integrity and many other features. Practically every modern customer-grade PC contains software for communicating over TCP/IP which makes it ideal for interfacing between a very open-ended user machine and vehicle. UDP is the sister protocol to TCP and is necessary for smooth integration with an Internet-like environment. One may have TCP without UDP or even IP, or any combination but for communication with PC:s they are all needed and should be implemented together in a bundle. The bundle of the Internet Protocol Suite and all other protocols and algorithms for communicating over the Internet is sometimes referred to as "Internetworks", hence the title of this document.The Internet Protocol suite will most likely be implemented in-vehicle as a result of a series of various factors, such as: law requirements regarding vehicle diagnosis, demands for higher Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU bandwidth due to growth in ECU software and not least connectivity with customer applications.There are many TCP/IP stacks available with various licenses and openness ranging from the very permissive to closed. In short, there is an abundance of mature available implementations that can, and should, be used.This document will sometimes mention the underlying physical layers, but most of the requirements in this document should be considered generally valid for most high-speed physical layers with some modifications. Requirements for bandwidth / throughput are NOT specified by this document, but will rather be defined by either the physical layer specification and / or the application layer specification.The Open System Interconnection Reference Model (OSI Reference Model or OSI Model) is an abstract description for layered communications and computer network protocol design. The Internet Protocol Suite defines only the Network (IP) and Transport Layer (TCP/UDP). OSI Model Specification Coverage Application Presentation Session Transport(TCP, UDP) Internetworks General Specification Network(IP, ARP, ICMP, IGMP) Data Link Layer(802.1Q) Ethernet Datalink Layer Physical Layer(802.3) Ethernet Physical Layer Relation between the OSI model and the specification coverage.TCP, UDP and IP may be considered very mature protocols and have been deployed in a wide range of systems. However, they are quite complex and there is an abundance of extensions and protocols working on the different levels in the OSI model in order to maximize performance and reliability of the network. Many of these, such as ARP will be loosely specified in this document with references to their respective specification. The requirements in this document apply to all ECUs that use TCP/IP/UDP in the vehicle network. This specification is to be regarded as a minimum that all TCP/IP/UDP ECUs must implement.4.3.12.1.1.1 Definitions & Abbreviations Abbr. This is done with a min and max values. Integer is always transferred as a unsigned number as "the actual number" – "the min value". Both min and max could be negative. ENUMERATION This is handled as an integer but with defined names. It could have a size constraint, but would otherwise be as small as needed, depending on the number of values declared. Tip: To improve readability of a packed message it's often a good idea (if minimal packed size is not a goal) to aim for byte aligned sizes, i.e. to constrain the enumeration to (0..255) BOOLEAN One bit of data, that's all. OCTET STRING An array of bytes, that always has a size constraint. The size is always coded directly in-front of the byte array. This is the closest thing to a string, and this compiler always decodes this data onto a buffer with one extra byte that is zero. It's thereby accessible as a string even though it might not be printable characters inside. An OCTET STRING member must be manipulated using the specific ASN_Octet_String ``` GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No493(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU functions and is not accessible as direct as the other primitive types.UTF8StringUTF8String is in essence the same as an OCTET STRING, but where the name indicates the type of content.NULLNULL is a special type indicating that an object exists but has no data. Mostly used in CHOICE constructs.Ellipsis Extensibility Marker “...”The ellipsis “...” is mostly used as the last element in a SEQUENCE, where it indicates that the sequence may later be extended with more elements. The construction makes it possible for an extended message to be backwards compatible with receivers who do not know about the extension. Any new elements must then be added after the extension mark.OBS: MSWord often autoconverts the three dots “...” into the single character “...” which will not be understood by the code generator.Make your own types – your building blocksThe type-name of any defined ASN.1 object must start with a capital letter. The name of the elements within a defined type must start with a lowercase character.SEQUENCE – The structThis is a simple “container class”. The elements are coded in the order they are stated in the definition, but the sequence in itself does not encode to any data. I.e. it is only a convenient way of collecting several other elements.Elements could be OPTIONAL. The standard of PER encoding states that the needed flags (one bit each) should be coded at the beginning of each sequence. This compiler makes it possible to place the flag wherever needed; as long as it’s before the element it referees too.CHOICE – The unionOnly one of the elements inside a choice will be encode/ decoded, based on the choice. The choice value (or type field) is always encoded first followed by the chosen element. There is a size constraint on the choice declaring how many bits to use for the choice field and thereby how many different elements you can have.In the standard there are no way of declaring the value of each choice, but that is added to this compiler. Otherwise you would be forced to declare 255 NULL values to be able to handle a message type filed of one byte and declaring message number 255.SEQUENCE OF – The arrayThis type declares an array of either another defined type, or an array of any build-in types.4.3.13.1.1.3 Introduction to Using the Normal MessageThe serialization is based on the parameter list defined by the IP bus message.The IP bus message defines the exact position of all parameters in the payload and has to consider the memory alignment.The serializer shall implement an alignment of 1 byte. Its purpose is to clarify the path taken by the message.Receive:Low level message handling.4.3.13.1.2 RequirementsThe Internetwork specification [Internetworks General Specification] and IP Routing specification [IP Routing Specification] defines a set of rules that must be considered and fulfilled when designing/using the IP Command Protocol and the control signals used by the applications (which is handled in separate documents).Design Rule:If applications (proprietary) intend to communicate internally within the vehicle network between IP based ECU's and when there is a need of a control channel, this specification (IP Command Protocol) shall be used. If the application under development is based on a well known protocol (standardized framework), this should be stated in the corresponding IP Signal Content specification (SWRS) and does not need to use the IP Command Protocol. Example the usage of FTP (RFC-959) would mean that this specification is not needed.There is a set of specification which shall be used together:The IP Command Protocol which contains requirements and design guidelines which must be used for the implementations.The IP Command Bus which defines services which is offered by servers. The IP Command Bus may generate a set of source-code files which shall be used for the implementations of the services. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU The IP Command Protocol defines controlling mechanisms which are suitable for IP-based(capable) networks (e.g. Ethernet STP, USB, APIX2 or MOST150). This means that the IPCommand Protocol is independent of the physical communication bus, as long as thecommunication bus has support for Ethernet. title: Process-flag, proc
body: 1310 v1Process-flag, proc Version history:(1):Purpose: To define the usage of the process flagSource:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 381652v0The proc -flag is 1 bit and shall have the default value 0x0. It defines an alternative handling procedure by a server. Messages (with operationIDs) that initiate a time consuming process at the server shall have this flag set to 1 to make the server keep track of the message. The proc -flag applies only for messages with operation types Request and SetRequest, since the message flows includes a Response that may take more or less time for the server to send back to the client. Only the function designer shall decide if this flag should be set to 0x1 for a particular message. If a message of a type other than Request or SetRequest in combination with proc-flag set to 0x1 is received the server shall continue processing the message as if the proc-flag was set 0.A state Processing shall be defined for the alternative handling process of messages where the proc -flag is relevant. The handling process shall enter this state when the message has been acknowledged and exit when the Response message has been sent. While in this state the server shall responde with an ERROR message with error code processing according to [REQPROD 381391]. Figure: An Illustration of the Processing state when an incoming request is acknowledged and later respondedNote: An example is shown in [REQPROD 346841] but it is valid also for [REQPROD 346844], [REQPROD 346849] and [REQPROD 346850].

title: ProtocolVersion
