body: 1523 v1 AT4 Wireless Performc Tool Version history:(1): Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Purpose: To define one of the tools which the OEM uses for attribute performance measurements, which works on android, ios, windows (arm,x86/x64, Windows Phone), Linux (x86/x64, arm), MAC OS and is used in various testphases.Source: https://www.at4wireless.com/Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 419491v0The supplier shall guarantee/enable that the AT4-agents part (client and server) of the AT4-Wireless Performance tool is able to read out necessary Key Performance Indicators (KPI), AND that it's possible to read out L7 and L3 (according to AT4-wireless Performance tool).The following Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) is a minimum requirement:ThroughputLatency (One Way Delay)Jitter (Latency Variation)Packet lossTCP advanced statisticsCPUCurrent (mA)Power (mW)Battery Consumed (time - ms)UDP/TCP ThroughputUDP Packet Loss RateUDP Packet Loss PatternsUDP Latency (one-way)UDP JitterTCP RTTTCP ACKsTCP RetransmissionsTCP Windows SizeIP Packet statistics (size, inter arraival time, etc)UDP KPIs (according to AT4-wireless Performance Tool System Description)TCP KPIs (according to AT4-wireless Performance Tool System Description)Wi-Fi BSSIDWi-Fi ESSIDWi-Fi PHY RateWi-Fi RSSIWi-Fi RCPI (Received Channel Power Indicator)Wi-Fi FrequencyWi-Fi ChannelWi-Fi SNRNetwork Interfaces usageGPSWLAN roaming (time interval of each Wi-Fi association, BSSID/ESSID, Aaverage and Peak Throughput, Min / Max RSSI, Throughput at Min/Max RSSI, First / Last RSSI, Throughput at Min/Max RSSI, Min/Max SNR, Throughput at Min/Max SNR, First/Last Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU SNR.

title: Link Monitoring - Wireless links
body: 1525 v3 Link Monitoring - Wireless links Version history:(3):Purpose: To possess the link quality information for wireless links.Source: REQPROD 352558Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 352576v2The router ECU shall implement a feature to monitor the quality of the wireless communication links.The Link Monitoring for wireless links, shall set a number of parameters and counters defined in the table below: Parameter DescriptionMAC address of the external Access Point.If the wireless interface is not connected, this parameter should be set to 00:00:00:00:00:00. Access Point If the wireless interface is connected to an access point, the MAC address of the access point shall be presented.Overall quality of the link. May be based on the level of contention or interference, the bit or frame error rate, how good the received signal is, some timing synchronization, or other hardware metric.This is an aggregate value, and depends totally on the driver and hardware. Link Quality Signal Level Received signal strength (RSSI - how strong the received signal is).Metrics: dBm Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Noise Level Background noise level (when no packet is transmitted). Similar comments as for Signal level. Rx Invalid ID Number of packets received with a different SSID. Used to detect configuration problems or adjacent network existence (on the same frequency). Rx Invalid Crypt Number of packets that the hardware was unable to decrypt. This can be used to detect invalid encryption settings. Rx Invalid Frag Number of packets for which the hardware was not able to properly re-assemble the link layer fragments (most likely one was missing). Tx Excessive Retries Number of packets that the hardware failed to deliver. Most MAC protocols will retry the packet a number of times before giving up. Invalid Misc Other packets lost in relation with specific wireless operations. Missed Beacon Number of periodic beacons from the Cell or the Access Point which have been missed. Beacons are sent at regular intervals to maintain the cell coordination, failure to receive them usually indicates that the WLAN transceiver is out of range.

It shall be possible to enable or disable the usage of the application via local config file and parameter PerformanceTool.4.3.18.1.2.7 Wi-Fi Spectrum4.3.18.1.2.7.1 AP Channel Deployment Strategy4.3.18.1.2.7.1.1 AutomaticTo avoid channel overlapping the following channel strategy shall be used for the WLAN transceiver when used as AP. This deployment strategy shall be seen as a guideline, since there might be regional differences and existing wireless medium (WM) which might interfere with local channels in a specific frequency range. It's therefore important that each WLAN transceiver checks which country code that is used and the surrounding channels to minimize the risk of overlapping channels. Additionally, it's important to remember that overlapping may cause unacceptable degradation of signal quality and throughput. Example of channel deployment in 2.4GHz with no overlapping channelsThere are two ways to deploy channels, either use "auto channel mechanism" (tries to select the best available channel by scanning all channels) or use static channels (the same channel after every reboot, at all time).The WLAN transceiver shall support both mechanisms but only one can be used at a time. Due to potential co-existence problems with Bluetooth, it's recommended there is an arbitration mechanism to exchanges channel occupancy data between the WLAN AP and Bluetooth.A potential issue with the dynamic approach of selecting clean channels could be a co-existence with Bluetooth. An alternative approach is to always use same (static) channel for the WLAN whenever AP is deployed at an ECU; this makes it easier for Bluetooth to always avoid a certain area on the ISM frequency band.If a default WLAN channel is chosen and if this channel encounters interference from other WLAN devices, the user shall consider changing the channel up or down to avoid the interference. This is functional requirements which are not covered within this specification. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU

title: Channel Interference Avoidance - Auto Channel
body: 1528 v4 Channel Interference Avoidance - Auto Channel Version history:(4):Purpose: To ensure that overlapping channels are avoided and to maximize the data throughput of the WM, channel deployment strategy is necessary. title: Selecting and advertising new channel
body: 1530 v1 Selecting and advertising new channel Version history:(i):Purpose: For an AP, if the channels are to congested the AP may attempt to move a BSS to a new operating channel.Source: Chapter 10.9.8.2 in [WLAN Phy DL Ex 2]Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 429242v0The WLAN transceiver configured as AP shall be able to:· to detect the surrounding channel congestion by using passive scan· if a cleaner channel (than current) has been detected for time x (configurable via Local Config Data file) and the channel satisfies applicable regulatory requirements AND if there are associated STA (supporting the new proposed clean channel)· The AP may take the decision to switch channel, but first informing the associated STAs that the AP is moving to a new channel and maintain the association by advertising the switch using Channel Switch Announcement elements in beacons frames.· The AP may force STAs in the BSS to stop transmissions until the channel switch takes place by setting the Channel Switch Mode field in the Channel Switch Announcement element to 1. title: Operating across regulatory domains
body: 1536 v1 Operating across regulatory domains Version history:(1):Purpose: The vehicle is a mobile device which are able to cross countries/domains and violate regulations. Beacon frames contains information on the country code, max allowable transmit power and the channels that may be used for the regulatory domain.Source: Chapter 9.18 in [WLAN Ex 2]Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 429467v0The WLAN transceiver and application shall be able to get country information and adopt the PHY to the country/region/domain to avoid violations via either:[1] external interfaces, such as GPS information.[2] periodic scan (with minimum performance degradation if used by applications) and search for beacons containing country string information.dot11MultiDomainCapabilityActivated is true (according to REQPROD 431685 and REQPROD 429203)Example:Scan and collect country information from beacons. If x beacons of multiple APs are using a new country string, the WLAN PHY shall adjust to the new country/region/domain.If no beacons are detected containing, country information, the WLAN application shall use current country/region/domain code.4.3.18.1.2.8 WLAN Network TypesBasic Service Set (BSS) is the basic building block of 802.11 networks. Basic service set is a group of devices which can communicate to each other when in the communication range.There are two types of Basic service sets defined by 802.11 standards.Infrastructure BSSIn Infrastructure BSS, stations cannot communicate to each other directly (unless IEEE 802.11z is supported) and have to go through access point. This also means that communicating devices do not need be in direct range of each other. They just need to be in communication range of access point increasing communication range of basic service set (BSS). Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU As all communication is relayed through access point, it takes more transmission capacity when compared to Independent BSS but it also reduces complexity of PHY layer as STA are not required to keep database of neighbouring STAs relationships within basic service set (BSS).Also, access point is in better position to assist STAs who want to save power by monitoring their state and buffering frames for STAs while STAs are in power save mode. Independent BSSIn Independent BSS, devices/stations can communicate to each other directly and hence needs to be in communication range of each other. Typically independent BSS are set up temporarily and teared down when purpose is accomplished. So generally Independent BSS are short lived. Independent BSS are also called Ad-hoc BSS or Ad-hoc network. Extended Service SetIEEE802.11 standard provides a way to link multiple BSSs to form a larger Extended Service Set (ESS). ESS is generally created by linking multiple BSSs to a backbone network. All linked BSSs in ESS share same SSID i.e. network name.STAs which are on same ESS can communicate to each other using backbone network (Distribution system). A large ESS enables the possibility for STAs to no be confined to a smaller coverage area of single BSS and roam free within ESS without losing connectivity to network. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 4.3.18.1.2.8.1 ESS

title: Local Configuration data
body: 1541 v2 Local Configuration data Version history:(2):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 358936v0It's required that the supplier provides a Local Configuration Data file and a Local Configuration Tool that enables the modification of the parameters within the Local Configuration Data file.The Local Configuration Data file content (Factory default settings) contains a mix of default parameters (to be used at start up): Parameter Default Value DescriptionDefault P2P SSID for the Wi-Fi Direct to usewhen configured as P2P GO according to REQPROD 358678. P2P GO SSID 4.3.18.2.2.1 Wi-Fi Peer-to-PeerIEEE802.11 standard though has a provision to create device to device Ad-hoc network; has limitations and drawbacks e.g. lack of efficient power saving support and QoS capabilities. Because of these limitations, Ad-hoc mode from IEEE802.11 standard has never been able to grab a market attention.IEEE802.11z TDLS amendment to standard though enabled setup of physical link between two stations; is still limited by requiring stations being connected to same Access Point.Hence to make direct device to device connection possible, Wi-Fi Direct technology defined by Wi-Fi Alliance, builds on top of IEEE802.11 infrastructure mode instead of Ad-hoc mode and enables direct device to device communication without a need of an Access Point.Unlike IEEE802.11 Infrastructure network, Access Point and Station roles in Wi-Fi Direct technology are dynamic, and are negotiated during group formation phase of connection.Peer-to-Peer technology contains three components:P2P DeviceSupports both P2P Group Owner and P2P Client roles and negotiates roles during Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Group formation phase of connection.○ May support WLAN and P2P concurrent operation○ Supports WSC and P2P discovery● P2P Group Owner (GO) role○ P2P Group Owner works like Access Point in infrastructure mode.○ Implements "registrar" role of WSC functionality○ P2P Group Owner may also support communication between associated clients● P2P Client role○ Works like STA in infrastructure network to implement non-AP features of infrastructure mode.○ Implements "enrollee" role of WSC functionality.P2P topologyP2P topology is 1:n where client devices can connect to a single Group Owner (GO) to form a group. Clients in P2P Group can be either a legacy device (device not supporting WiFi P2P standard) or a P2P Client. P2P Group has a single SSID and provides one security domain. P2P Components and topologySource: WFA P2P spec v1.2A P2P Device can support concurrent operation with WLAN infrastructure network while being a member of a P2P Group. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU P2P GroupP2P DeviceP2P Device P2P Concurrent deviceSource: WFA P2P spec v1.2A P2P Group can operate on same channel as of WLAN infrastructure network or on a different channel. It is also possible that P2P group and concurrent WLAN Infrastructure network operates in different frequency bands viz. 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

title: P2P Persistent Groups
body: 1553 v1 P2P Persistent Groups Version history:(1):Purpose: To invoke P2P Group between two devices which were members of group previouslySource: Wi-Fi Peer-to-Peer (P2P) technical specification v1.2Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 358558v0 P2P Device shall support formation of P2P Persistent group.4.3.18.2.2.1.2.3 P2P Power savingIEEE802.11 standard defines power saving mechanisms but they are mainly intended for devices in STA role. Standard do not specify power saving mechanism for devices in Access Point role.WFA Peer-to-Peer specification specifies two new power saving modes for P2P Group owners to allow them to be absent for defined period in order to save power.Opportunistic Power Save (OppPS):This mode allows Group Owners (GO) to take opportunity to save power if all associated P2P clients are sleeping. For some reason, if any of the associated P2P client devices do not go to sleep, then P2P Group Owner cannot sleep and hence this power saving mechanism yields less power saving for P2P Group Owner.To save power, P2P Group Owner defines CTWindow period for which it will be available after each Beacon instant. P2P Devices are allowed to transmit in CTWindow period. If at the end of CTWindow, if all associated P2P Clients go to sleep then, P2P Group Owner can sleep until next Beacon instant. Otherwise Group Owner need to stay awake until next Beacon instant. ![](images/23e55a23e0832480f410925f9101b83b54b8a64891d98f9dd2d60c74d2386099.jpg) Figure - P2P Group Owner Opportunistic Power Save (source: WFA P2P spec v1.2) ## · Notice of Absence (NOA): o This mode allows P2P Group Owner to announce period of absence through Beacon frames or Probe responses, where associated P2P Clients are not allowed to access channel. o A P2P Group Owner can either cancel or update the current NoA schedule at any time by respectively omitting or modifying the signaling element. P2P Clients always adhere to the most recently received NoA schedule. o P2P Group Owner defines Notice of Absence schedule using 4 parameters o Duration - specifies length of absence period o Interval - specifies time between consecutive absence period Time - specifies the start time of the first absence period after the current Beacon frame o Count - No. of how many absence periods will be scheduled during the current NoA schedule GEELY Geely Automotive Research Institute (Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document Type Note-SWRS Document Release Status RELEASED Document No Revision 005 Volume No 01 Page No 675(1572) Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU Figure - P2P Group Owner Notice of Absence (source: WFA P2P spec v1.2)

title: Support for Legacy device
body: 1555 v1 Support for Legacy device Version history: (1): Purpose: To ensure that legacy devices are able to connect to P2P group Source: Wi-Fi Peer-to-Peer (P2P) technical specification v1.2 Verification Method: Analysis Legacy ID: 358658v0 Implementation shall support operation of legacy devices (device not implementing WFA P2P Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU technology) in P2P group, together with other P2P devices.4.3.18.3 WLAN Security4.3.18.3.1 Appendix A - Possible threatsThis appendix shall be seen as an acknowledgement that there are several threats on the WLAN link that should be handled by a WLAN system (STA, AP, AS).4.3.18.3.1.1 DoS Attack 1By utilizing a wireless transmitter an attacker could effectively launch a DoS attack by jamming the channel used by the system. At least this would cause a serious performance hit to the system because of the CSMA/CA technique used in IEEE 802.11 networks. The impact of this attack could be reduced by changing the AP channel, however this will probably cause synchronization issues between ECU and AP, furthermore the attacker can also change channel.4.3.18.3.1.2 DoS Attack 2A second DoS attack is possible by injecting forged management frames on the network (these frames are always sent unprotected on the network), e.g. deauthentication or disassociation frames. This is possible by injecting a packet that seems to originate from the AP (by using the APs MAC-address as sender address in the MAC-header) which will force the ECU to reauthenticate or reassociate.4.3.18.3.1.3 DoS Attack 3 - Memory Exhaustion AttackBecause the first message of the 4-way handshake is not authenticated (this is before PTK generation) it is open for spoof attacks. The ECU has to store all received messages 1s and the generated PTK associated with it until positive confirmation from the AP in message 3. An attacker could continuously generate false message 1s in the 4-way handshake process, potentially causing memory exhaustion in the ECU.4.3.18.3.1.4 Evil Twin AttackIt is possible to set up another AP with the same SSID as the real network, tricking ECUs to connect to the rogue AP instead of the real one. Combined with a fake AS this could be a serious security threat. To fight this type of attack or at least reduce its impact, it is imperative that the ECU only exchange information with an AS that present a known and valid certificate. By just tricking ECUs to connect to a rogue AP however the attacker has successfully launched a type of DoS attack effectively stopping ECUs from accessing the real network.4.3.18.3.1.4.1 Rogue APEven with the chosen RSN architecture using EAP-TLS an attacker can set up a fake AP, which mirrors the SSID, encryption type and band. It's possible for the attacker to configure the fake AP to capture and record all authentication requests. The attacker then waits for the user to attach to the fake network and captures their credentials and it's possible that the attacker may crack the challenge/response pair to recover the password.4.3.18.3.1.5 Other AttacksSeveral other attacks are possible for pre-RSNA algorithms such as WEP or the less secure RSNA-PSK (WPA-PSK/TKIP/RC4) mode. As the use of these methods are prohibited according to this specification, the potential attacks are not further investigated here. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 4.3.18.3.1.6 Packet modification attacksThe integrity protection of EAP-TLS packets does not extend to the EAP header fields (Code, Identifier, and Length) or the Type or Flags fields. As a result, these fields can be modified by an attacker.In most cases, modification of the Code or Identifier fields will only result in a denial-of-service attack. However, an attacker can add additional data to an EAP-TLS packet so as to cause it to be longer than implied by the Length field. EAP peers, authenticators, or servers that do not check for this could be vulnerable to a buffer overrun.4.3.18.3.1.7 Spoofing and hijackingGain access to privileged data and resources in the network by assuming the identity of a valid user.4.3.18.3.1.7.1 Stolen CertificatesIt is imperative that the certificates are protected from access by a third party both from unauthorized access in the ECU both also by implementing a well-constructed PKI and CA hierarchy. Certificates must only be awarded to well trusted entities in a controlled environment. A stolen certificate is not enough to gain network access as each certificate is also associated with a unique username and password. It is however likely that if an attacker is able to steal a certificate it is probably also possible for him to get access to the associated credentials. The good news is that as all certificates are unique, they could easily be revoked by the AS and denied access to the network in the event of a security leak. The problem is to know when a certificate has been compromised. As the network probably shouldn't be used for general purpose activities, one way to detect unauthorized usage could be to analyze network traffic. If a client cannot be identified by application systems it is probably not allowed on the network.4.3.18.3.2 RequirementsThis section details the specific requirements regarding the use of the IEEE 802.11 network.4.3.18.3.2.1 Data ConfidentialityThere are various encryption methods available, which are based on different algorithms. The IEEE 802.11-2007 provides three cryptographic algorithms to protect data traffic: WEP, TKIP and CCMP, where WEP and TKIP are based on the RC4 algorithm and CCMP based on the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm. According to IEEE 802.11i, WPA shall be seen as an intermediate solution to WEP insecurities. WPA implemented a subset of a draft of 802.11i and WPA2 implements the mandatory elements of 802.11i and uses the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). WPA2 is backwards compatible with WPA and the primary difference between WPA and WPA2 is the type of encryption used; RC4 and AES respectively. WPA2 has replaced WPA. The table below shows the most frequently used encryption standards and how they apply to the WLAN transceiver in the vehicle. Encryption Standard WLAN Data Encryption Rules Open ( no encryption )WEP - ( RC4 based algorithm )WPA - TKIP ( RC4 based algorithm ) Not Allowed WPA2 - CCMP ( AES based algorithm ) Allowed GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No678(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Table: Supported WLAN Data Encryptions in vehicle

title: Data Confidentiality - Policies
body: 1558 v3 Data Confidentiality - Policies Version history:(3):Purpose: To ensure a high level of security (only authorized users may access the network).Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 55088v2The data confidentiality shall be ensured by following the Policies according to the tablePolicies - Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 in section Scenario mapping – Policies .4.3.18.3.2.2 Probe RequestsA normal connection procedure is initiated by a periodic transmission of beacon frames from an AP. This beacon contains network information such as SSID, RSN information, the APs MAC-address etc. An alternative approach is that the ECU broadcasts probe request frames to find active APs in the vicinity of the ECU. Receiving APs will respond with a probe response frame which contains much of the same information as a beacon frame. What is important to realize is that both the ECU and the AP transmits their respective MAC-address as part of the MAC-header in all communication. Periodic probe requests by the ECU should therefore not be used to avoid the possibility of a third party tracking the ECU. The MAC-address only uniquely identifies the hardware in a specific car and not the person driving it and to get a detailed position is quite complex. Nevertheless, periodic transmission of beacon frames from an AP should be enough to get a fast and reliable connection.

title: Probe Requests
body: 1559 v2 Probe Requests Version history:(2):Purpose: All packages sent on the network include the sender address in the MAC header. Due to this, probe requests should not be transmitted by the ECU. Connection attempts shall only be made after receiving an appropriate network beacon.Source: IEEE Standard for Information technology - Telecommunications and information exchange between systems - Local and metropolitan area networks - Specific requirements, Part 11: Wireless LAN Medium Access Control (MAC) and Physical Layer (PHY) Specifications, Clause 7.1, WLAN Security Requirements - External publications; WLAN Physical & DataLink Specification, WLAN Security RequirementsVerification Method: Test Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Legacy ID: 55112v1Do not use probe requests (active method). Applies to WLAN Transceiver (ECU).4.3.18.3.2.3 Regional SecurityThe Chinese broadband wireless IP standard working group has developed a standard named WLAN Authentication and Privacy Infrastructure (WAPI) or GB 15629.11-2003.WAPI is a security model and patent contributed by IWNCOMM for WLAN. To ensure support for Chinese products, the WLAN transceivers used for this market needs to support WAPI.

title: WLAN Authentication and Privacy Infrastructure (WAPI)
body: 1560 v3 WLAN Authentication and Privacy Infrastructure (WAPI) Version history:(3):Purpose: To ensure that the WAPI standard for the Chinese market is fulfilled.Source: GB 15629.11-2003, ISO/IEC WD 20011 Alternative security mechanism for use with ISO/IEC 8802-11.Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 55114v2For the Chinese market, WAPI shall be used.4.3.18.3.2.4 RSN ArchitectureThe RSN architecture as specified in IEEE Std 802.11-2007 consists of the following steps:Initial authentication and association between STA and APAuthentication using Pre-Shared Key (PSK) or IEEE Std 802.1X-2004A 4-way handshake between STA and APWhen a STA (Wi-Fi client) want to connect to a network it has to perform an authentication and association request with an AP that belongs to the network. This step is performed regardless if the RSN architecture is used or not. The authentication is in this step performed by Open System Authentication (OSA) and has nothing to do with security. The WLAN device (e.g. ECU) supplies an ID and the AP accept or deny the connection based on policy, not identity. After association is performed the two parts have also negotiated which security policy to use for the rest of the communication. See the figure below for an overview of the connection establishment. ![](images/dd2f6c60c9453c627280583fb0cb1ff64946b706efeff7f174e092ce9cddce5b.jpg) Geely Automotive Research Institute (Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No681(1572) Base Tech SWRS DHU Figure: Establishing the IEEE 802.11 association An RSNA can be made by IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 authentication or PSK. Regardless of authentication method the RSN architecture specifies that a 4-way handshake should take place between STA and AP. The purpose of the 4-way handshake is to do the following: · Confirm that a live peer holds the Pairwise Master Key (PMK) · Confirm that the PMK is current · Derive a fresh Pairwise Transient Key (PTK) from the PMK · Install the pairwise encryption and integrity keys · Transport the Group Temporal Key (GTK) from AP to STA · Confirm the cipher suite selection GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No682(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure: Establishing pairwise and group keys using IEEE 802.1XAccording to the figure Establishing pairwise and group keys using IEEE 802.1X above, the PMK is used to generate a PTK which in turn is used to derive a set of keys used for data integrity and encryption in Unicast communication. A GTK is used for encryption of multicast communication. If IEEE 802.1X is used, a successful 4-way handshake means that an encrypted link is established and the logical IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 controlled port is opened for normal network traffic. This could be interpreted as comparable confidentiality as to a wired connection. This has nothing to do with internal security on the network though which should be handled by higher layer protocols and is not related to link security.IEEE Std 802.11-2007 does not prohibit STAs from simultaneously operating pre-RSNA and RSNA algorithms, however to ensure the security of the network,onlyRSNA algorithms should be used.1561 v2 RSN ArchitectureVersion history:(2):Purpose: IEEE Std 802.11-2007 defines two classes of security algorithms, RSNA algorithms and Pre-RSNA algorithms. To reach the desired level of confidentiality for the IEEE 802.11 network, RSNA should be used.Source: IEEE Std 802.11-2007 Clause 8.1Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 55082v1 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU RSNA algorithms shall be used exclusively. Applies to Vehicle WLAN transceiver (ECU configured as STA or AP) and by all external AP that are used to communicate with the vehicle.4.3.18.3.2.5 Scenario APSK is used in WPA2 Personal and is as the name suggests intended for home or SoHo use. The PSK system uses a preloaded password consisting of 8-63 ASCII characters for mutual authentication. The password is the basis for the PMK and is shared among all entities across the network. In other words, all network security is based on the confidentiality of a single password. Furthermore all connecting clients who provide the correct password are trusted and no further inspection of their identity is made. This implies that to be able to deny access on a per client basis, the password for all other APs and clients would have to be changed. Weak passwords may also be subject to brute force attacks using information sent during the 4-way handshake.

title: IEEE 802.11 Default Passphrase
body: 1562 v3 IEEE 802.11 Default Passphrase Version history:(3):Purpose: To ensure that there is a default passphrase for the WLAN transceiver when WPA2-PSK is used. By default, the passphrase shall be unique for each vehicle by adding a random number to the passphrase and based on approved algorithms from the NIST standards.Source: [WLAN Sec 8], [WLAN Sec 9]Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 55108v2The default passphrase shall be set to a random unpredictable passphrase using t he Random Number Generator (RNG) which uses strong PRNGs based on NIST SP 800-90 standards.1. The Deterministic Pseudo Random Number Generator (DPRNG) used for generating any cryptographic keys (such as private keys, passwords, session keys, etc.) must comply with NIST SP 800-90 standards.2. The DPRNG used for generating any cryptographic keys (such as private keys, passwords, session keys, etc.) must be initialised with a sufficient amount of entropy from an entropy pool.3. The sources for entropy pool must have an non-deterministic behaviour. Valid entropy sources may be:○ Injected entropy during production (note, needs to be unique per device)○ System interrupt timings that are not deterministic (such as user input)○ Noise on physical processes (such as temperature measurement, sound input, etc.)4. The current state of entropy pool shall be persistent between system boots in-order to have an early high quality entropy.

title: Roaming Authentication
body: 1572 v3 Roaming Authentication Version history:(3):Purpose: To ensure a smooth roaming between APs if the vehicle is moving within a wireless medium. This requirement is valid for scenario B.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 89523v2It's required that the WLAN transceiver supports STA roaming within an ESS meanwhile providing full security and as low roaming latency as possible. The device shall support the usage of preauthentication. The process of finding and re-associating new APs includes:·scan for available access points·compile a list of roam targets·pick the best access point from the list of roam targets.It's required that the supplier consults with the OEM regarding the best solution for a efficient roaming. Roaming criterias needs to be discussed (e.g if the signal strength is 20% stronger Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU than current AP),4.3.18.3.2.6.2 IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 AuthenticationTo cover the scenario B where a vehicle connects to an external AP, Authentication using IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 should be used. The standard describes the connections between STA, AP and AS and introduces the concept of two separate logical ports on both STA (supplicant) and AP (authenticator). One of the ports, the uncontrolled port is normally open and only allows traffic that is needed for authentication. The second port, the controlled port is used for normal network traffic and is only opened after a successful authentication procedure. The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) protocol is used in the authentication stage or rather Extensible Authentication Protocol Over LANs (EAPOL). EAPOL however is just a messaging format and relies on several different so called methods for the actual security. IEEE Std 802.11-2007 does not specify a mandatory EAP method but does state that the method used have to support mutual authentication. Figure: The authorization state of the controlled port.The AS contains a database of allowed users on the network and is a central part in IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 authentication. The authentication procedure is started by an identity request from the authenticator (AP) to the supplicant (client). The authenticator relays this information to the AS which allow or deny access based on identity information supplied through used EAP method. It is important that the AS also proves its identity in this stage to ensure that the STA (Vehicle ECU) only attach itself to authorized networks. The AS should be one or more centrally accessed servers that are able to provide authentication services to all connected workshops etc. The communication link between authenticator and AS have to be secure as this is a prerequisite for the entire RSN architecture. During the authentication procedure a PMK is generated by supplicant and AS. This PMK is later transmitted from AS to authenticator and is used to generate all further encryption keys.After a successful authentication procedure a 4-way handshake is initiated as detailed above. A successful authentication could be compared to the physical connection of a client to a wired network, the ECU is still not allowed to use the network.See the figure below for an overview of the 802.1 x EAP authentication procedures. Figure: IEEE 802.1X EAP authentication

title: General Security
body: 1575 v3 General Security Version history:(3):Purpose: To ensure that the highest possible security is achieved for using the IEEE802.11 technology.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 55078v2It's required that the supplier of the WLAN transceiver consults (with the OEM) and documentspotential flaws or weaknesses of chosen security mechanisms. The supplier is required toinform the OEM, if/when the chosen standard security mechanism is breached or cracked andneeds to be updated.4.3.18.3.3 IntroductionThis document specifies all security related requirements that shall be implemented to get a secure connection on the link layer between an Access Point (AP) and a wireless station (STA).The WLAN transceiver within the vehicle may be used as either AP or STA. This documentspecifies security requirements both on the ECU containing the WLAN interface as well as on Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU the access point that the vehicle shall be able to connect to.The document is intended for the developers of the component that provide a WLAN link between the vehicle and networks outside of the vehicle. That includes networks at manufacturing sites, service and aftermarket sites and PD development sites. The developer may be an external supplier or an internal software department. The document is also intended for tool vendors that will provide equipment that will be used at manufacturing sites, at service and aftermarket sites and during internal development within PD to diagnosis and download software to ECUs within the vehicle. The third group that this document is intended for are those within cars that are providing it-infrastructure to manufacturing sites, service and aftermarket sites, and PD. If the software product is a part of a larger system and interacts with other software products, this document also should be read and approved by the system designers and the designers responsible for each interacting software product.IEEE Std 802.11i-2004 (amendment to IEEE Std 802.11-1999) introduced a new security architecture named Robust Security Network (RSN). This amendment relies on IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 and was issued to remedy security concerns regarding wireless connections as detailed in IEEE Std 802.11-1999. That particular standard relies on WEP for confidentiality purposes, a now deprecated pre-RSN algorithm which can be cracked in a matter of minutes using widely available tools.IEEE Std 802.11i-2004 is now a part of the updated IEEE Std 802.11-2007 which is the current standard for WLAN communication and the basis for this specification. The standard specifies the PHY and MAC layer according to the OSI model. The security aspects detailed for the ECU in this document is relevant for the MAC layer and does not rely on a specific PHY layer.Certain communication protocol discussed for other entities in this documents are implemented in higher layers e.g. AP-to-AS communication.All commercially available WLAN-equipment is normally certified by the Wi-Fi Alliance. The commercial name for a full implementation of IEEE Std 802.11i-2004 is called WPA2 Personal (PSK) or WPA2 Enterprise (IEEE Std 802.1X-2004 authentication). All equipment carrying Wi-Fi certification sold after 2006 have to support at least WPA2 personal.The purpose of this document is to define how the RSN architecture should be used to reach a comparable level of confidentiality on a wireless link as to a wired connection. Furthermore, this document intends to support various VCC scenarios where one WLAN transceiver (in the vehicle) will be used for two scenarios with different purpose (Access Point or Station). Extra care has to be taken, since the internal WLAN transceiver shall cover two security strategies (methods). The two figures below, covers the scenarios where the WLAN transceiver is either acting as Station (STA) or Access Point (AP).The first figure below covers one scenario when the WLAN transceiver is configured as AP and nomadic devices, configured as STA connects to the AP. Another solution is that the vehicle WLAN transceiver is configured as STA and connects to one nomadic device which operates as AP, to e.g. provide internet access. WLAN security used two parts: Authentication and privacy (encryption). WPA-v2 (802.11i), Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) and 802.1x are parts of the strongest security that is available today, for a setup when there is no need for an authentication server. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure: “Scenario A”, Example where Nomadic devices connects to the vehicle WLAN transceiver configured as AP.In the second figure, when the WLAN transceiver is configured as STA, the intention is to connect the vehicle to a known external AP which requires a high security level. For certain scenarios, the usage of authentication servers (AS) enforces strong security and access policies like time-of-day access. Figure: “Scenario B”, Vehicle connected to external network equipment.Important to note is that this document only specifies the security of the wireless link, sabotage of the medium or the WLAN technology is still possible. An attacker could for example use an "evil twin" i.e. a rogue AP that share SSID with the real network. If this evil twin transmits at a higher power, ECUs will try to connect to that AP instead of the real one, effectively blocking the real connection. In fact, this evil twin could also extract sensitive information from the ECU if adequate steps are not taken (e.g. mutual authentication using known certificates). A connection could also be attacked by in-band interference or DoS-attacks by injecting packets on the network e.g. de-authentication requests. This document does not cover all security strategies that must be considered and deployed at external wireless networks (outside the vehicle). However, external wireless networks must consider deploying wireless IDS which can detect, de-authentication attacks, RTS and CTS denial of service attacks and Rouge APs. Security Access Level Purpose Comment 01 Used for software download A vehicle unique security access constant shall be generated in the manufacturing process. 03 Car mode transition A common security access constant shall be applied. 05 General for diagnostic services This is the default area that shall be applied by the ECU, unless there is a specific need to separate the specific information from others. 11 Immo. - - - - 1D Test and development only Uses the algorithm supported by OEM tool-chain (but not used at manufacturing or workshops) 1F Legal requirements for ERA-GLONASS - - 31 Vehicle Speed Limitation 5F Pyrotechnic end-of-life activation ISO 26021 requirement Table - Security Access Levels4.4.3.1.4 IntroductionPurposeThe purpose of this document is to define the security algorithm to be used with diagnostic service $27 (request security access) for all ECUs supporting diagnostics, regardless of protocol. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Diagnostic service $27 is based upon the tester requesting a random three byte seed from the ECU. The tester then utilizes the algorithm described in this document to calculate a three byte key which is transmitted to the ECU. The ECU utilizes the same algorithm and compares its calculated three byte key to the key submitted by the tester to determine if security access is granted or not.The algorithm described in this document generates a three byte response (key) to an eight byte challenge. The eight byte challenge consists of three random seed bytes (S1, S2, S3) and five fixed bytes (F1, F2, F3, F4, F5). Note that the five fixed bytes are not transmitted on the network and must be known in advance by both the ECU and tester. These fixed bytes are also referred to as the Security Constant.The seed bytes are transmitted from S1 (most significant byte of the 3 byte seed) to S3 (least significant byte of the 3 byte seed) in a $67 positive response to a service $27 (security access) diagnostic request. For example, $67 $01 $S1 $S2 $S3.Key (response) bytes are transmitted from R1 (most significant byte of the 3 byte key) to R3 (least significant byte of the 3 byte key) in a $27 submit key request. For example, $27 $02 $R1 $R2 $R3.4.4.3.1.5 Algorithm Description

body: 1590 v2Fixed Bytes default valueVersion history: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU (2): Change the Verification Method from Test to Analysis Purpose: To define the default value of the fixed bytes when no Security Constant has been programmed to the ECU.Source: Required by diagnostic tools.Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 353877v0ASIL: QM - Not safety relevant If the fixed bytes has not yet been programmed to the ECU and unlocking by the $27 Security Access service is requested, the ECU shall use a default value where all fixed bytes are set to 0xFF.

title: Key Storage
body: 1591 v1 Key Storage Version history:(1):Purpose: The security of the system depends on the secrecy of the key that is used.Source:Verification Method: Test + InspectionLegacy ID: 360246v0The Fixed Bytes used shall be stored in a protected area, typically in tamper resistant memory, and must not be possible to read out. If a key update process is required, the security of that process must be ensured. 4.4.4 Software Authentication 4.4.4.1 General Software Authentication 4.4.4.1.1 System DescriptionTo support legacy systems and enable future growth, the Software Authentication concept must be prepared to support several signing methods even though an ECU will only support one. The defined signing method will affect:Algorithms and key lengths chosenSign and verify with code signing certificates or by only using the key-pair (no certificates)How to transfer the signature dataHow to initiate the verification in the ECU and inform the user of the result...Software Authentication Generation 2.0 - each software part is signed individually:Each software part is signed individually and each software part is carrying the digital signature, separately generated as previously shown in Figure - Software signing function overview. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure - Software signing of each software part independentlyFor off-board tool reference purposes (to manage the variability), the legacy concept "Software Authentication Generation 1.0 (Legacy) - complete set of software parts are signed" can be found in [Software Authentication].This section will describe the following main parts, for the method where each software part is signed individually:Software part creationResponsible: ECU Software SupplierSignResponsible: Trust CentreSoftware DownloadVerification Figure - Create, Sign, Download and Verify a software part4.4.4.1.1.1 Create Software PartA software part could be segmented into several data blocks. To verify the data stored, the ECU must have knowledge of the data that must be verified and where it is located. TheECU software supplier will, once the application is build, generate a Verification Block Tableand append it to the Software Part. This block table contains information of all other data blocks (location and hash values), i.e. it is equivalent to a manifest. The Verification Block Table Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU will be digitally signed and when the ECU has verified it, the ECU could continue to verify all other expected data blocks. Hence, there will be one Verification Block Table per Software Part. Figure - Verification Block Table formatExample.The ECU software supplier has build an application having two data blocks.Based on the two data blocks, the ECU software supplier generates and adds a Verification Block Table (a dedicated data block, stored at a known start address):The start address, length and hash value of the Verification Block table itself are added to the file header. The hash values of the data blocks stored in the Verification Block Table are calculated on the data only, but the hash value of the Verification Block Table (i.e.verification_block_root_hash in software part header) is calculated using also its start address and length. Note that the lengths defined in the VBT are the lengths of the data blocks prior to e.g. any compression is applied.4.4.4.1.1.1.1 Verification Block Table

title: Format of the Verification Block Table
body: 1600 v5 Format of the Verification Block Table Version history:(5): ClarificationPurpose: Define the format of the verification block tableSource:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 398360v4The verification block table, encoded with big endian, shall have the following format:Verification Block Table Format Identifier. The verification block will start with most significant byte of this format identifier. It defines the version of the verification block table, mainly intended for tool parsing and format checks in the ECU, i.e. it shall not be used to configure e.g. the actual algorithm to be used by the bootloader. Size 16 bits.Number of data blocks. This shall be identical to the number of data blocks included in the software part. The data block containing the verification block table itself shall not be Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU included. Size 16 bits.StartAddress [ size 32 bits], Length [ size 32 bits], Hash value. Every data blocks shall be defined, except the block table itself. The size of the hash is dependent of the hash function used and is specified elsewhere. The Length is the unprocessed length (see other requirements for more details).The data blocks shall be sorted according to the order the data blocks are being programmed to the ECU.Example.SHA-256 hash function is used, i.e. each hash value is 256 bits.Number of data blocks are two, i.e. the total length of the verification block table, in octets, will be (16+16+2x(256+32+32))/8=84 octets. abc HeaderBlock 0x00060000Block 0x00060100Block 0x0007FF00StartAddressLengthDataCheckSum 0000 : 00 00 00 02 00 06 00 00 00 00 00 13 D7 8E CD 620010 : C6 2C F1 F5 75 D7 DE C6 D2 FD 57 DA 06 65 54 FD0020 : 42 EE E5 C8 67 E7 00 83 BC 94 22 62 00 06 01 000030 : 00 01 EF 00 E6 02 7B 3F 95 9F AF 23 1B 38 2F FD0040 : C6 4E B2 38 25 E6 B7 CC EA 47 F5 19 6D 02 CA 2A0050 : FD F4 41 88 Figure - Example of a VBF file with a verification block tableFigure - Example of a VBF file with a verification block table shows a software part (VBF data file). title: Verification Block Table - Input order to Hash function per data block
body: 1602 v2Verification Block Table - Input order to Hash function per data block Version history:(2):Purpose:Define the input order to the hash function per data block. If the order is changed, the output from the hash function will be changed also.The start address and length of a data block are NOT input to the hash function. title: Verification Block Root Hash
body: 1601 v4Verification Block Root Hash Version history:(4): ClarificationPurpose:Define how to calculate the verification block root hash, carrying the information of unprocessed data that is required to support use cases of having processing methods not necessarily known to the Trust Centre.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 404694v2 Req:The verification_block_root_hash must be calculated on the "raw" unprocessed data in the verification block table, i.e. when no prior to any padding, encryption/compression/delta encoding method hasmethods have been applied to the VBT data block. The verification block root hash shall be calculated as Hash(startAddress||length||Verification Block Table data), where || represents the concatenation. The order shall be according to Figure - Verification Block Root Hash calculation. The start address (verification_block_start) and length Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU (verification_block_length) are included to ensure the placement of the verification block and shall always be 32 bits long each. The (root) hash function shall be the same as used when calculating the hash value of the data blocks defined in the verification block table (REQPROD 404696).Start Address Length DataData byte #1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ... Data byte xstartAddress Byte, MSB startAddress Byte, LSB Length Byte, MSB Length Byte, LSB Data Byte, first Data Byte xFigure - Verification Block Root Hash calculationThe root hash value shall be added by the software supplier to the header of the software part.Example 1.All values are in hexadecimal. SHA-256 is used as hash function.Hash(startAddress||length||Verification Block Table data)=Hash( 00 05 FF 0000 00 00 54 00 00 00 02 00 00 F0 00 00 00 00 88 B7 07 24 15 45 A3 46 26 5A AB 1F FB 32 FF 64 B5 5B F8 F8 DC 1B 56 A4 6E F3 3C E3 D1 5D B1 1D 33 00 00 F1 00 00 00 10 5A 2C FE 8A B9 35 91 85 25 D4 4F D6 FD 87 C7 0F C8 3B 4F 29 D1 A7 27 67 2E 1B 48 F3 80 47 3F C1)=9B B4 E0 92 1C 4B 84 1C 31 C3 CB 3F DD 15 D0 B9 E8 ED 70 5E D3 C2 52 DC C9 2A D5 06 E0 5E 2B AE.Start Address: 0005FF00Length: 00000054Data: 00 00 00 02 00 00 F0 00 00 00 00 88 B7 07 24 15 45 A3 46 26 5A AB 1F FB 32 FF 64 B5 5B F8 F8 DC 1B 56 A4 6E F3 3C E1 5D B1 1D 33 00 00 F1 00 00 00 00 10 5A 2C FE 8A B9 35 91 85 25 D4 4F D6 FD 87 C7 0F C8 3B 4F 29 D1 A7 27 67 2E 1B 48 F3 80 47 3F C1Example 2.The length of the data block for a verification block table is 44 bytes long, prior to any padding or processing method is applied.All data blocks shall be aligned to a multiple of 8 bytes. Hence, the VBT data block is padded to 48 bytes, but verification_block_length is still 44 (0x2C). It is this length that is used when calculating the verification_block_root_hash.Note: Be aware of the differences of how to manage the padding of data and start/length information for data blocks that are defined in the verification block table versus the data block containing the VBT.

body: 1606 v3 Verification Block Table per Software Part Version history:(3): Change the Verification Method from Test to AnalysisPurpose: To enable that each software part is to be signed and verified individually.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 398371v1Each single software part must contain a verification block table, i.e. it will be one verification block per logical block defined in the ECU. 130849 v1 Verification Block Table in a padded data block Version history:(1): NEWPurpose: To clarify how to manage the verification block table when there is a need to Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU align that data block to a specific length, e.g. to match the start and/or end of a data block to the boundary of a flash sector (for an addressed based ECU). This requirement is valid for the data block containing the VBT, i.e. for all other data blocks the padding will be treated as any other data when generating the VBT.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 457183v0Req:If there is a must to align and pad the data blocks to some specific size, the padded data must have the value of erased memory, i.e. it will be included in the ECU "blank" check. Figure - Data block with aligned verification block table data blockNote: The verification Block Table_block_start, verification_block_length and verification_block_root_hash shall be calculated on data (blocks)generated using the "raw" unprocessed data in the verification block table prior to some processing methods have beenany padding is applied, i.e. prior to the any compression, encryption or delta encoding is applied to this specific data block.4.4.4.1.1.2 Sign Software PartThe software is signed with theconfidentialprivate key. It is the Verification Block Table that is signed, as defined by the software part header identifier. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure - Software Signing ToolThere are many use-cases to be supported, including different diagnostic clients, in order to download (signed) software to a vehicle:- key balancing, e.g. having global/common keys used for a period of time or ECU unique keys- software download at manufacturing, workshops, over-the-air (including vehicle internal tester), test&development, fault-tracking (e.g. when a software download using workshop diagnostic client fails and R&D tools must be used), repair analysis etc. Figure - Example of entities downloading software to a vehicleTo support the variability as shown in Figure - Example of entities downloading software to a vehicle as well as balancing key usage, the signature data for production (e.g. customer vehicles) vehicle is kept detached (separate file).Example.Unique keys are used.A software application 12345678AA.vbf is to be signed using private key#1 for ECU#1 and private key#2 for ECU#2. The sw application part could be programmed in both ECUs but the belonging signature data must be transferred to the correct ECU respectively, otherwise the application will not start. Document NamePage Tech SWRS DHH Figure - Example: Detached signatureThe Figure - Example: Detached signature shows the principle of detached production signature.Hence, the diagnostic client must have the capability to correlate belonging signature for a software part and transfer it to the vehicle. Download software part number 12345678AATransfer signature data for software partnumber 12345678AADownload software part number 87654321BBTransfer signature data for software partnumber 87654321BB Figure - Download a software and transfer signature dataTo support the test&development phases, a development key-pair will be used. To simplify the software part management, the software signature for development will be placed in the part header (the R&D diagnostic client will also have the capability to read the software signature for production from the software part header [VBF (Versatile Binary Format) ]).Refer to section Key Management for Test and Production ECUs for further details. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU

title: Signing function - Integrity Check
body: 1613 v2 Signing function - Integrity Check Version history:(2):Purpose: To ensure that the software part is not altered when updated, i.e. validate the integrity.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 428664v1The signing tool used must ensure the integrity of the software part. If the tool is updating some software part identifier, the file_checksum shall be checked before and after the update and the checksum shall be identical.

title: Sign Software Part - Private Key syntax
body: 1611 v3 Sign Software Part - Private Key syntax Version history:(3): Change the Verification Method from Test to AnalysisPurpose: Define the key representation for key distribution at test&development and for development tool usage.Source: PKCS #8: Private-Key Information Syntax Standard, RSA Laboratories Technical Note Version 1.2, Revised November 1, 1993. PKCS #1 v2.2: RSA Cryptography Standard, RSA Laboratories, October 27, 2012. RFC1421.Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 428665v1The Private key shall be represented in an unencrypted PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo format as defined in PKCS #8: Private-Key Information Syntax Standard, RSA Laboratories Technical Note Version 1.2, Revised November 1, 1993.The PrivateKey part of the PrivateKeyInfo shall be a represented as an ASN.1 type RSAPrivateKey as defined in PKCS #1 v2.2: RSA Cryptography Standard, RSA Laboratories, October 27, 2012.The Private Key shall be stored using the PEM format (base64 encoded data) as defined in RFC1421.Note: This is the formats to (at least) be supported by signing development tool. The format used by the Trust Centre (production) is specified elsewhere.

title: Signing function - Generate signature
body: 1612 v4 Signing function - Generate signature Version history:(4): ClarificationPurpose: Define the input data to the signing function.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 428667v3 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU The data to be signed is defined by the verification_block_start and verification_block_length identifiers. These start address, length and data of the addressed data block shall be used as inputs when generating the hash value. The signing entity has two possibilities:(1) always calculate the hash value over the verification block table and ensure that the content of the table is correct. This is the preferred option.(2) use the already calculated hash value (verification_block_root_hash).Example.The verification_block_root_hash might be used when the processing method is not known (e.g. delta compression method) as defined by the software part data format identifier but it might also be used to optimize off-board functions (e.g. computational time), alternatively when the verification_block_start and verification_block_length are not present in data file header. Sign - Processing method unknown

title: Append signature to software part
body: 1610 v5 Append signature to software part Version history:(5): ClarificationPurpose: Define how to append the signature to the software part. The signing tools must support the use-case of sign and re-sign software parts, typically during development but also to enable for e.g. key updates. To support the lifecycle of the part, i.e. the software is verified (development) prior to it is released to production, two signature types will be applicable for the final software part (to not have to re-sign the software when it is to be used in a test object versus a production vehicle).Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 428666v2The digital signature when the software part is signed with the intended private key fordevelopment, sw_signature_dev, shall be appended to the software part header by the software supplier when a part is delivered.. The resulting sw_signature signed by the trust centre at OEM with the intended key forproductionshall be stored in a separate file, using a standardized format separately (e.g. .xml). The signing tool must support both sign and re-sign functionality of a software part.Example.(1) A software part is delivered containing the sw_signature_dev. This software can only be GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No727(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHUused in an ECU equipped with the public key for development.(2) The software part is, when successfully verified, validated and ready for production, signed with the private key for production. This means that two signatures are present (the sw_signature_dev is kept).(3) This software part can now be used in both a development and production ECUs, but it must be ensured that the corresponding signature is transferred at SWDL. Figure - Signature for test and development and production4.4.4.1.1.2.1 Sign and verify unprocessed dataAt the ECU side (where the software part is verified) it is the target data to be executed that shall be verified, e.g. the data stored in the non-volatile memory (for an application file). Hence, it is the unprocessed data that must be signed, i.e. the data prior to any processing method ( delta encoding, compression, encryption, etc.) has been applied. Figure - Signing and verification of unprocessed (target) data Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU From an ECU point of view, see Figure - Verification of unprocessed data, where the data stored in the non-volatile memory is verified, Figure - Verification of unprocessed data

title: Sign and verify unprocessed data
body: 1615 v2 Sign and verify unprocessed data Version history:(2): Change the Verification Method from Test to Analysis Purpose: Define how to handle compressed, encrypted or delta encoded software.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 404594v0 The signing and verification shall be based on unprocessed data. 4.4.4.1.1.2.2 Sign a Delta Software PartWhen delta encoding is used, the delta file shall contain information (hash values, signature, ... ) identical to the final target software: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU A programming of this delta file (version 1.9 is already installed) will result in the same final target image as when the Full Version 2.0 file is programmed.Figure - Signature for a delta fileWhen a delta file, as shown in Figure - Signature for a delta file is programmed, the ECU must finally verify the final data that has been installed in the non-volatile memory.

title: Sign a delta file
body: 1614 v5 Sign a delta file Version history:(5): ClarificationPurpose: Define how to sign a delta file. The programmed (installed) data shall be verified, i.e. not the transferred (streamed) data.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 429082v3A delta software part shall contain the same header identifiers as the corresponding full version, with respect to following Software Authentication identifiers: verification_block_start, verification_block_length, verification_block_root_hash and sw_signature_dev.4.4.4.1.1.3 Download a (signed) software partThis section describes how to download a signed software part and transfer the signature data, where the signature data is transferred aftereachsoftware part is downloaded. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Addressed based data storage ECUErase MemoryRequest DownloadTransfer DataRequest Transfer ExitCheck MemoryComplete and CompatibleECU ResetECU implementing CheckMemory does not include a CheckSum in the response parameter.Routine Control CheckMemory("software signature"), i.e. transfer the signature for development or production. The tester could do two consecutive attempts.A condition for being complete is that CheckMemory is passed. Figure - SWDL of a signed software partThe software signature is transferred when the complete data file has been downloaded using the CheckMemory routine control, which will also initiate the ECU verification. The result values provided in the CheckMemory response will inform the tester whether the verification has passed or not . Note that ECUs implementing CheckMemory shall not respond with a checksum value at the RequestTransferExit service. The CheckMemory return values are specified in [General Bootloader requirements]. The result value is 0 (zero) when the verification is passed. If the verification is failed, the tester might do a second attempt.Prior to the programming of a data file starts it must be ensured that the expected public key is stored in the ECU, e.g. either an initial development key is stored and to be kept (test and development only) or the dedicated public key shall be programmed (if it is not already programmed).4.4.4.1.1.4 Verify a signed software partThis section describes and defines the general ECU verification requirements, relevant to both off- and on-board (ECU) systems. More detailed ECU requirements are however part of [General Bootloader requirements].An ECU is divided into several "Logical Blocks", one logical block per software part and each logical block is signed/verified independently. A successful signature verification means that a logical block is complete (complete & compatible). The ECU must know the logical blocks that are mandatory for the whole application to be complete.The logical block definition, ECU Software Structure, is to be re-programmable in order to support use-case when the software structure is changed from e.g. three to four files or when a software part growths beyond its dedicated range. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure - ECU Software Structure, ESSThe programmed public key is used to verify the software part, i.e. the logical block at:Installation, i.e. at Software Download (must).But, the memory not changed (e.g. memory not used for adaptations, "user space", etc.) after e.g. software download can also be verified:At every start of the application (secure boot), starting from a root of trust and trusted read-only start-up code.At run-time, i.e. when the application is running.A software part must have been verified OK for the application to be started in the ECU. The secondary bootloader, stored in volatile memory, is not shown in Figure - ECU Software Structure, ESS. The SBL must be successfully verified prior to it is activated.4.4.4.1.1.5 Key Management for Test and production ECUsTo e.g. simplify the daily life for developers/testers etc. and to keep track of the keys used for signing and verification during test and development, a known key is used. This must not be used in production vehicles.An empty (e.g. spare part) ECU shall by default contain the defined development key. The initial development key is used to verify software until the production key has been programmed to the ECU (WriteDataByIdentifier). Hence, a transition from that initial development key to a production key must be supported. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure - Transition from Development to ProductionTo simplify fault tracking, but also to ensure the integrity of the public key when it is programmed for production, a checksum of the public key will be appended when it is stored. That checksum is also possible to read once a public key has been successfully been programmed (i.e. it is not possible to read the checksum when an initial development key has been stored in the ECU by the ECU provider).To prepare for future growth, where even more additional metadata will be appended to the public key to e.g. support a layered key structure, the term Public Key Type is used. That is used to e.g. inform the trust centre about the key structure supported by the ECU but could also be used by the diagnostic clients programming the public key (and metadata) if there is a need to store future public key types differently (e.g. using different diagnostic services).Example - Public Key Types.PublicKeyModulusPublicKeyExponentPublicKeyCheckSumType 1PublicKeyModulusPublicKeyExponentPublicKeyCheckSum"Some more metadata"Type 2Figure - Public Key TypesThe first type in Figure - Public Key Types is the format defined in the Software Settings File section by the swAuthPublicKeyType as RAW_KEY_WITH_CHECKSUM.1607 v1Production Key programmingVersion history:(1): Delete the requirement "Production Key programming";Purpose: To ensure that no production vehicle leaves manufacturing or workshops Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU equipped with a development key. A development key is to be considered as known, i.e. it adds no security value.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 435017v0It must be ensured that no production vehicles leaves the plant or workshop equipped with the development key, i.e. a valid public key for production shall be programmed to the ECU. This is applicable also for the use-case when no software part at all is being programmed at End-of-Line (e.g. an ECU is pre-programmed with the software, replaced etc.).This requirement is not applicable for the ECU supplier but for off-board systems where the vehicle is manufactured (or at workshops).

title: Signing Method - Variability control
body: 1599 v4 Signing Method - Variability controlVersion history:(4): ClarificationPurpose: To control the variability at the back-end systems but also to inform the ECU ofthe signing method (at design time) that shall be applied. Note that a specificECU does not have to support all methods, but only one. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 404595v3To define and distribute the Signing Method, a Software Settings File (a software part) shall be used for methods where each software part is signed individually.Note: The notation, e.g.SHA256_RSA2048_sw_part is used in nextcoming requirements to define algorithms to be applied. The "sw_part" is used to separate this method from legacy concepts. See also section "Software Settings File" actual definitions.

title: Default Signing Method
body: 1598 v2 Default Signing Method Version history:(2): Change the Verification Method from Test to AnalysisPurpose: Define the default signing method. The ECU shall use the default signing method, unless else is explicitly defined elsewhere, e.g. in the LC : Diagnostics and ECU Platform.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 410732v0The default signing method shall be SHA256_RSA2048_sw_part_based.4.4.4.1.2.2 Signing Method - Algorithm Definitions

title: Signing Method SHA256_RSA2048 - Hash function
body: 1594 v2 Signing Method SHA256_RSA2048 - Hash function Version history:(2): Change the Verification Method from Test to AnalysisPurpose: Define the hash function.Source: FIPS PUB 180-4, Secure Hash Standard (SHS) FEDERAL INFORMATION PROCESSING STANDARDS PUBLICATION, March 2012.Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 404598v0The hash function to be used is the SHA-256 (256 bits) as defined in FIPS PUB 180-4, Secure Hash Standard (SHS), March 2012.

title: Signing Method SHA256_RSA2048 - Public Key Algorithm
body: 1596 v3 Signing Method SHA256_RSA2048 - Public Key Algorithm Version history:(3): Change the Verification Method from Test to AnalysisPurpose: Define the public key algorithm.Source: PKCS #1 v2.2: RSA Cryptography Standard, RSA Laboratories, October 27, 2012Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 404620v1 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU The public key algorithm shall be: PKCS #1 v2.2: RSA Cryptography Standard, RSA Laboratories, October 27, 2012, where the RSASSA-PSS signature scheme shall be used. The signature scheme includes a salt when generating a signature. The salt length shall be set to the same length as the underlying hash value. This means that the resulting signature will be different every time a file is signed.

title: Signing Method SHA256_RSA2048 - Key Size
body: 1595 v2 Signing Method SHA256_RSA2048 - Key Size Version history:(2): Change the Verification Method from Test to Analysis Purpose: Define the key size for the private- and public key.Source: PKCS #1 v2.2: RSA Cryptography Standard, RSA Laboratories, October 27, 2012Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 404623v0 The key size shall be 2048 bits. This is the size of the modulus part of the key representations. 4.4.4.1.2.3 Signing Method - Key balancingThe software authentication concept must support different strategies with respect to key management and key balancing. Three main security classes with respect to software authenticity are defined in Table - Software Authentication security classes. After a threat and risk analysis the proper security class shall be defined and applied for ECUs in the vehicle platform(s). Based on that decision, the affected variant management systems shall be updated accordingly. Hence, both the signing method and key usage must be configurable. In case of an incident, or if a signing key for other reasons must be changed, the key must be able to change (when global keys are used).

title: Software authentication security classes
body: 1597 v3 Software authentication security classes Version history:(3): Clarification Purpose: To align the terminology but also describe the expected possibilities of how to balance the key usage. This variability must be managed in the variant handling systems off-board.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 441876v1 The software authentication security classes as defined in the Table - Software Authentication security classes must be supported with respect to key management. This means that it shall be possible to configure the key usage in the off-board variant management systems:1) Integrity check only, i.e. no cryptographic keys needed2) ECU global keys used for a period of time. This shall be applied by default.3) ECU unique keys Security Class – SoftwareAuthentication Meaning GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No740(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU SwAuth Class 1 Integrity check only, i.e. only using checksums/hash values, for error detection.This is not part of the General Software Authentication document, but added here for legacy reasons. SwAuth Class 2 Authenticity (origin + integrity), using common/global keys.A dedicated signing key per ECU type shall anyhow be applied, e.g. one for all door modules and another for the climate control respectively (for segmentation)The key used shall be possible to change after a period of time (structure week) and (optional) vehicle type. SwAuth Class 3 Authenticity + “copy between vehicles protection”.An ECU unique key shall be applied.This class is recommended for sellable features but also for risk reduction (e.g. a key is revealed).SwAuth Class 3 shall always be applied when there is device unique keys for diagnostic service securityAccess, for programming services. B4 87) 4.4.4.1.4 Definitions and Abbreviations Definition Description Authentication Authentication is the process of assuring and verifying authenticity. Authenticity The property of being genuine and being able to be verified and trusted. Digital Signature Used to assure originator authenticity and data integrity (of a software) Hash Hash algorithms are also called digital fingerprinting algorithms. They are irreversible functions that provide a fixed-size hash based on various inputs. Irreversibility and collision resistance are necessary attributes for successful hash functions.Examples of hash functions are Secure Hash Algorithm 2 Integrity The property that specified information remains unchanged between observations Key-pair The key-pair is used with a public key algorithm. The private key, which is secret, and the public key, which is publicly available. The private and public keys are cryptographically related. The private key cannot be derived from the public key. The private key can be used only by its owner, and the public key can be used by third parties to perform operations with the key owner. Trust Anchor The public key of trusted entity (root Certificate Authority certificate or the public key only) Trust Centre A trusted party of the public key infrastructure, including key management systems, with a central authority.
