body: 6446 v4 Remove Debug Functionality Version history:(4):Purpose: Ensure no backdoors are left open Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID:Ensure that all hardware or software debugging tools used during development are removed and cannot be used to circumvent any security mechanisms.Debug functionality shall be removed on all systems produced or intended for end customer use.Any software debug services must be removed and it is not sufficient to block access using a filter and firewall rule.HW debug interfaces shall be removed or permanently disabled by e.g. burning a fuseThe supplier must confirm and if possible prove that all debug functionality is removed before delivering production systems.Any deviations shall be approved by Geely/CEVT security staff. 116133 v1 Secure Defaults Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: InspectionLegacy ID:The ECU shall enforce the security by default principle where there is no functionality accessible without consistency with the CEVT/GRI security requirements (zero access by default). Any deviations must be approved by CEVT/GRI Security team. 116134 v1 Cryptographic Algorithms Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Usage of cryptographic algorithms in the ECU shall follow industry standards and best practices and no proprietary solutions whatsoever are accepted. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 116135 v1 Secure Systems Modification Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Any changes to the system shall maintain the ECU security with respect to the security requirements or policies of the CEVT/GRI. This will ensure that upgrades or modifications will not transfer the ECU to an insecure mode. 116136 v1 Performance Security Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Security mechanisms should be designed in such a way that do not degrade the system performance unnecessarily. For example, using hardware support or efficient security solution to consider the overhead of the security operations during the design. 116137 v1 Incident Patch Management Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:During the entire ECU life cycle, any discovered security risks or incidents shall be promptly reported to CEVT/GRI.The supplier is responsible to continuously and actively find and analyze any cyber security vulnerabilities or risks affecting the integrity of the delivered system. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Any highly critical patch shall be in place within one week after being discovered or published.A security patch process and strategy shall be presented by the supplierAnd make sure be aligned with the latest.<Security Patch Management Process with OTA>.If a fix is not available, a workaround may be applied where possible.When over-the-air updates are not available, a plan for legacy, physical critical security updates should be considered.Disclosure of any vulnerabilities of components must be approved by GRI cybersecurity team.4.4.7.2 Cyber Security Requirements for Security Level 2 ECUs4.4.7.2.1 General Requirements

title: Industry Standards
body: 6443 v3 Industry Standards Version history:(3):Purpose: Ensure a good security process for developmentSource:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID:Cyber Security must be part of the design and development processSystems and applications shall be developed in accordance with an appointed industry security standard or guidelines (e.g. OWASP, NIST or ISO27001) and follow any legal or compliance obligations applicable. Main objectives are to maintain confidentiality, integrity and availability for vehicle information security.The way of work shall correspond to "SAE J3061 - CyberSecurity Guidebook for Cyber-Physical Vehicle systems" and must be presented by the supplier covering:Guiding Principles in the Cyber Security WorkOverall management of Cyber SecurityCyber Security Life Cycle ProcessesSecurity StandardsApplications and programming interfaces shall be developed, deployed and tested in accordance with leading industry security standards, such as POSIX. The contractor shall be able to present Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU the way of working to ensure application and code security, such as program language coding guidelines.

title: Least Necessary Privilege
body: 6456 v3 Least Necessary Privilege Version history:(3):Purpose: Do not use higher permissions than neededSource:Verification Method: DocumentationLegacy ID:Every function and every user of the system shall operate using the least set of privileges necessary (the most restrictive) for the minimum amount of time to complete the job. Primarily this principle limits the damage that can result from an accident, error or unauthorized use by protecting user computations from each other.Each user, process or program shall only have the least amount of privilege required to perform their tasks. This encompasses user rights, resource permissions such as CPU limits, memory, network, and file system permissions.This concept shall apply to both systems and operations/users. System functions such as read, write and execute should be separated. System operations and users roles should be as separate as possible.The used methods for authorization and access control shall follow industry best practice. There shall be a written Access Control Policy to ensure that the chosen access control functionality is designed and implemented in a consistent manner.Usage of Superuser accounts, such as” root”, shall be avoided for all processes, applications, system access and user privileges.Technologies / Solutions to implement secure access control may include the usage of solutions such as, but not limited to; SELinux (https://www.selinuxproject.org), Tomoyo (https://tomoyo.osdn.jp), AppArmor (https://gitlab.com/apparmor/apparmor/wikis/home/).

title: Event logging
body: 6512 v4 Event logging Version history:(4): Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Purpose: Log security events using a common log formatSource:Verification Method: InspectionLegacy ID:If the ECU supports logging, security event logs shall be included in the log file according to the specification in this requirement.The exact details of what to be logged needs to be agreed between the supplier and the GRI/CEVT depending of the ECU functionality and usage.Any major events like software updates, high privilege system access, changes to encryption keys or important system events shall be logged.Passwords shall not be written to the log and any sensitive data or personal information shall be anonymized or encrypted.If the ECU contains system time, the log entry shall be time stamped to support reconstruction of activity timelines.Hardware limits or other circumstances may affect the storage size but if nothing else is specified, the log buffer shall be sized to allow storage of at least 1000 messages and a FIFO strategy shall be appliedIf no log format is specified in other requirements or by the supplier, it is suggested to follow the Syslog format according to below examples and defined by RFC 5424 including priority, time, ECU identifier, severity level, facility and event description.Example:Time shall be given in UTC with the format:E.g. 2017-02-23T23:20:50ZThe message corresponds to the following format:VERSION TIMESTAMP HOSTNAME APPLICATION PID MESSAGEID STRUCTURED-DATA MSGThe following is a sample syslog message:<34>1 2017-02-23T23:20:50Z IHU su - ID47 - BOM'su root' failed for lonvick on /dev/pts/8If the same message is logged multiple times in a short period of time it shall be possible to rate limit the individual message to prevent filling up the log. Number of rate limited messages for a specific event during the last 10 seconds shall be appended to the MSG field of the log. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 1 2003-10-11T22:14:15Z IHU su - ID47 - BOM'su root' failed for lonvick on /dev/pts/8 ratelimited 34 events last 10sAll logged events shall be protected securely against unauthorized access. 116141 v1 Default Access Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:All access to the system shall follow the zero-access by default. Zero-access by default entails no access or virtually no access by default. All subsequent access shall be traceable back through an approval process. 116146 v1 Holistic Solution Alignment Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Component security should be aligned with any supporting infrastructure such as PKI and cloud security solutions. Cloud security requirements are described in a separate document and may vary in different geographic regions.PKI based solutions are used for secure communications and support for industry standards for distribution, creation, use, storage and revocation are expected. In particular, but not limited to PKCS (Public-Key Cryptography Standards), elliptic curve algorithms and OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) stapling. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 4.4.7.2.2 System Security 32331 v3 Software Signing and Verification Version history:(3):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Authenticity of any downloadable content shall be verified to avoid executing a malicious software and ensure information security for the execution environment.Any executables, data or applications being pushed or fetched from systems outside the ECU is treated as downloadable content.An electronic signature shall be attached and verified for any downloadable executable software's so that when users installs or upgrades them, the system can confirm that they are from a reliable source. 116142 v1 Software signing and authentication - authenticity Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Authenticity of any downloadable content shall be ensured to avoid executing a malicious software and to strengthen/harden the security for the execution environment.Any executables, data or applications being pushed or fetched from systems outside the ECU is treated as downloadable content.An electronic signature shall be attached to be verified for any downloadable software prior to any installation or upgrade. This will ensure that the downloaded file is from a genuine source. 116144 v1 Software Signing and Verification- Integrity Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Legacy ID:Accuracy and completeness' of downloadable shall be ensured through preventing unauthorized modifications. Any unauthorized modifications between source and destination of the downloadable shall be detected prior to installation or upgrade. For example, this can be done by verifying the digitally signed hash of the downloadable. 116145 v1 Software signing and verification - confidentiality Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:The content of the downloadable shall not be disclosed to unauthorized entities and it shall remain confidential. 4.4.7.3 Cyber Security Requirements for Security Level 3 ECUs4.4.7.3.1 General

title: Cyber Security Risk Assessment
body: 6461 v4 Cyber Security Risk Assessment Version history:(4):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID:A Cyber security risks assessment shall be done on the delivered system and presented to CEVT/GRI.HEAVENS shall be used as the risk assessment method and all underlying judgments and ratings shall be shared with CEVT/GRI. Templates will be provided by CEVT/GRI. Other risk assessment methods may be used after approval of CEVT/GRI Cyber Security team.The assessment shall consider threats against the ECU itself as well as any integration with other systems involved. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Risk shall be rated as high, medium or low and remediation activities or solutions shall be presented. The supplier is responsible to drive and follow up on any remediation activities. 116149 v1 Message Freshness Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:The ECU shall detect and deny that information received by any function at a given time is not a copy of the same information received at an earlier time by the same or another entity. 116150 v1 Handeling Malicious Events Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Any event that endangers the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system shall be denied by the ECU. 116151 v1 Security Verification Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:An appropriate test methodology such as OWASP Testing Guide or NIST SP 800-115 shall be used and described. The test methodology must be suitable for the target.Security testing of new or modified software that introduce a security risk shall be done continuously during the development and life cycle. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU All test cases and results shall be presented to CEVT/GRI.Mobile applications as well as the web applications running on connected ECUs and the Cloud APIs used by the applications should be tested according to the OWASP Testing Guide and OWASP Mobile Testing Guide.Cloud entry points and interfaces exposed by the vehicle should be tested according to NIST SP 800-115.The following verification methods shall be performed before each software release from the supplier.1. Fuzzing on all software than can be exposed to untrusted inputs Fuzzing test is a software testing technique that involves providing invalid, unexpected, or random data as inputs to a program. The program then is monitored for exceptions such as crashes or failing built-in code assertions or finding potential memory leaks. For the purpose of security, input that crosses a trust boundary is often the most interesting.2. Dynamic analysis3. Penetration testPenetration test is to guarantee that a completed program has less vulnerability. And all connected or exposed systems are expected to perform and present the result from a system vulnerability scanning followed up by a penetration test. The penetration testing shall be done by independent agency of the contractor's organization or a 3rd party.This requirement is in addition to the testing requirements defined in the Software Statement of Work and applies to any connected system that communicates with any external parties outside the vehicle such as Internet or cloud based solutions or applications. Some key component such as the nodes belong to basic control, expanded function (especially component that have connectivity feature), 3rd party application and some other component that is privacy sensitive should do penetration test and provide cybersecurity penetration report. 116153 v1 Operating System Security Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Secure operating system is an operating system that provides sufficient support for multilevel security and evidence of correctness to meet a particular set of requirements, which is a hardened operation system. A hardened microchip and a hardened operating system together make a really good solid platform that can defend infrastructures and protect key information in systems. The secure operation system shall be able to isolate some important components or subsystems, disconnect them from the Internet, or isolate physically from the outside world in some other way. Secure operation systems shall auto-configure all the privacy and security options and eliminate user's manual configuration. 116154 v1 Access Control Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:OS level access control. Authority setting and minimization. The process is to limit users and processes that can access resources or that can execute functions, as well as keeping permitted matters to a minimum. More about the concept can refer to SE-Linux, which perform access control based on the importance of each resource accessed at Linux Kernel level.Packet filtering. Packet filtering is to check communication data that flows through communication path or that arrived at the receiving end and then blocking communications that are not permitted. This can be used to prevent unauthorized access from the outside.Segmentation. Domain separation. Group a program's modules based on the criticality in terms of security and then restricting intergroup data exchange. This separates the parts affected by a failure or an attack from other parts.Network partitioning. Partition a network such as in-vehicle LAN based on the criticality in terms of security, and setting up a gateway in between to prevent unauthorized access. This separates the parts affected by a failure or an attack from other parts. 116155 v1 Authentication Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU User authentication. User authentication is to authenticate users and there should be measure taken to prevent brute force attacks.Server authentication. A client should also authenticate its server, the authentication process can prevent spoofing of serversEquipment and device authentication. It is to authenticate the communicating end, such as equipment/drivers and smartphone.In-vehicle equipment (ECU) authentication. There is no standard method to authenticate in-vehicle equipment. There are examples like EVITA HSM and TMP.Message authentication. Message authentication is to authenticate messages sent by the communication end, which help users to detect tampered messages and messages from a spoofed header.Program authentication. It is to authenticate programs within a system. One example is to attach electronic signature to executable programs so that when users installs or upgrades them, they can confirm that they are from a reliable source. It is to avoid executing a malicious program and ensure information security for the execution environment.4.4.7.3.2 Application Security

title: Enforce Secure Coding
body: 6523 v3Enforce Secure Coding Version history:(3):Purpose:Enforce secure codingSource:Verification Method:AnalysisLegacy ID:The secure coding requirements apply to the ECU system itself as well as for any On Board Application being hosted within the car.The supplier must ensure and continuously motivate the developers to seek higher knowledge within the security domain.All data input and output shall be validated (e.g. length, range and format checks) to prevent security issues due to systems errors, data corruption or misuse. There shall be a defined and predictable error handling to handle any exceptions and error states.Source code shall be verified by an automatic code review tool to achieve a high quality code. The supplier shall perform manual review on parts of code considered critical. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Special attention shall be given to avoid buffer overflows as well as authentication and access flaws. 116148 v1 Web Application Security Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:All web application development shall comply with mitigations of risks in the latest version of OWASP Top 10 Application Security Risks (http://www.owasp.org). 116152 v1 Application Security Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Application security refers to applications running on top of an operating system (such as Autosar or Linux). We should build the boundary between trusted and untrusted applications, and have the technology to prevent unauthorized access from untrusted world to the trusted one. Applications authorized by OEM and safety relevant are defined as trusted applications, otherwise untrusted ones. To reduce attack surface, containers may be used to enhance application sandboxing protection.4.4.7.4 Cyber Security Requirements for Security Level 4 ECUs4.4.7.4.1 Security Testing4.4.7.4.2 Application Security4.4.7.4.3 System Security

title: IDS and IPS
body: 6538 v3 IDS and IPS Version history:(3): Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Purpose: Prevent and detect intrusion attemptsSource:Verification Method: DemonstrationLegacy ID:A connected ECU shall have the capability to detect and prevent intrusions from networks such as Internet or a neighboring ECU. If any anomalies/attacks are detected these events must be logged and if possible mitigated.Attacks against the OS itself (e.g. Linux and Autosar), Streaming media, web traffic, onboard web apps, V2X, V2V and authentication mechanisms are of extra concern.Examples of behaviors that shall be detected and acted upon:1. Changes to important system files2. Traffic that violate IP or WiFi protocol standards3. Duplicate IP addresses or MAC addresses on connected networks4. Anomalies in statically analysis of number of packets seen on networks bus.5. Attacks towards services exposed by the ECU using well known attack signatures6. Authentication failures7. Unexpected traffic using a previously unused destination protocol or IP addressThe actions taken upon events shall be configurable to send an alarm, dropping detected malicious packets, resetting a connection or blocking traffic from the offending IP addressConfiguration of the IDS/IPS must be possible to perform from the cloud.To save performance it must be possible to configure what traffic and vulnerabilities the IDS/IPS are analyzing based on source, destination, protocol, type of attack and severity.The actions upon events shall be configurable per attack type to log, send an alarm, dropping detected malicious packets, resetting a connection or blocking traffic from the offending IP addressThere must be protection ensuring that IPS/IDS functionality never affects normal operation or functionality of the ECUThere shall exist a mechanism to self-protect/lock the device in case of cyber-attacks or malfunctions. In such event only traffic to configure and update the device shall be allowed. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU

title: Detailed Security Logging
body: 6724 v3Detailed Security Logging Version history:(3):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID:A detailed security audit log should be kept in the connected ECU. This requirement applies in addition to the security event logging requirements following RFC5424 that applies to all ECUs, unless other security audit logs are required by CEVT/GRI.It shall be possible to upload all on-board logs to a remote central cloud based solution for further diagnosis as well as:Remotely reset the on-board logsRemotely configure log parameters and settingsReceive IDSP/IPS logsDebug levelLimit local logging to configured security levels (Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Informational, Debug)Limit remote logging to configured security levels (Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Informational, Debug)Log protectionAll logs shall be encrypted when transported outside the ECUAll log files shall be encrypted when in restLog files may not contain passwordsPrivacy req followedSecurity Levels are defined according to RFC5424o Emergency: system is unusableAlert: action must be taken immediatelyCritical: critical conditions Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 3 Error: error conditions4 Warning: warning conditions5 Notice: normal but significant condition6 Informational: informational messages7 Debug: debug-level messagesInformation to be logged includes:a) User/car/ECU IDs;b) Dates, times, and details of key events, e.g. log-on and log-off;c) Terminal identity or location if possible)d) Records of successful and rejected system access attempts;e) Records of successful and rejected data and other resource access attempts;f) Changes to system configuration;g) Use of privileges;h) Use of system utilities and applications;i) Files accessed and the kind of access;j) Network addresses and protocols;k) Alarms raised by the access control system;l) Activation and de-activation of system services or deamonsAll logs shall be in RFC5424 syslog format and the structured data pair shall include at least the following information in the set order:VIN: VIN numberEcuID: Unique Identification ID (S/N) of ECUSource: Details about the origin of the attack, can be a adress, service, a user, a process and / or a nodeTarget: Details on the target of the attack can be a adress, service, a user, a process and / or a node and a file Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Action: Action taken (Drop, Log, Reject)Classification: Name of the attack and references, as CVEsSeverityLevel: Evaluation (also used in priority calculation) of the severity.)AdditionalData: Additional information on the attackAny additional information shall be added as separate fields after the AdditionalData fieldThe log buffer shall be sized to allow storage of at least 10000 messages and a FIFO strategy shall be applied.The following is a sample syslog message:<34>1 2017-02-23T23:20:50Z IHU su - ID47 [IDS_SDID@o vin="ABCDEFGH"ecuid="12345678" source="1.2.3.4" target="" action="block" classification="CVE-2017-0001" severity_level="warning" additional_data=""] BOM'su root exploitIf the same message is logged multiple times in a short period of time it shall be possible to rate limit the individual message to prevent filling up the log. The default rate limit period is 10 seconds but the parameter shall be configurable remotely. Number of rate limited messages for a specific event and time period shall be appended to the MSG field of the log.“ratelimited 34 events last 10s” 32329 v2 Separation of Connected and Vehicle Internal Systems Version history:(2): Change the Verification Method to AnalysisPurpose: Clear Security border between connected systems and systems connected to vehicle internal resourcesSource:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID:There must be a defined separation of connected systems in relation to vehicle systems connecting to vehicle internal interfaces or resources. Connected systems are more likely to be attacked and compromised. In the case of a compromised system there must be a second line of defense protecting further movements within the system to reach vehicle internal systems.There must be a hardware separation (or security wise equal solution approved by CEVT/GRI security team) using multiple CPUs to protect critical or safety related on-board of systems to be accessed by connected systems. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Systems (Vehicle Processor) having access to in-vehicle networks shall be separated from the processor running systems connected to off-board systems or downloadable apps/services (Application Processor).A well-defined protocol shall be used to communicate between the two processors so that it shall not be possible to set in-vehicle signals that is safety-critical for the driver during driving. An example of a well-defined protocol is CAN using a whitelist to restrict what signals that can be transmitted. 32330 v3 Secure Boot Version history:(3):Purpose:Source:Verification Method: DocumentationLegacy ID:The system requires that the boot process for all processors in the solution is secure and that security checks are made of the executed software in run time.The secure boot process must prevent the loading of drivers or OS loaders that are not signed with an acceptable digital signature.All software involved in the boot process must validate the integrity of the subsequent software to create an unbroken chain of trustDuring secure boot process there must not be any “escape sequences” to interrupt secure boot process. The system must not be booted from media which are attached to interfaces of the ECU. All external interfaces must be block for booting.The supplier must specify the whole secure boot procedure in detail. 116156 v1 Generic Exploit Mitigation Techniques Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID: Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Generic memory exploit mitigation techniques such as, but not limited to, force data execution prevention (DEP), address space layout randomization(ASLR), heap spray, null page protection, and return oriented programming(ROP-chains). 116157 v1 Firewall Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:Firewalls with stateful inspection must be used to control external interface(s) in the ECU. The vehicle networks shall be protected from other external networks through the use of firewalls. Firewalls should be configured to;- Deny network traffic by default and fail secure- Block network packets typically used to execute ‘denial of service’ attacks- Implement ingress and egress filtering, such as deny incoming and outgoing traffic where the source address is known to have been spoofed- Only allow communications based on specified source/destination IP addresses and ports based on application or based on content- All ports shall be closed except for those in a list of open ports, supplied separately depending of what feature and services that the ECU shall use provide/supportIt must be possible to update the firewall configuration (rule set etc.) remotely from the cloud. 116158 v1 Off-board communication security Version history:(1):Purpose:Source:Verification Method:Legacy ID:1 Identification, Authentication, AuthorizationThere shall be a mutual authentication process between the communication entities before the communication initializes. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Strong authentication methods must be used where adequate, as well as access control mechanisms. Passwords are managed accordingly.2 Secure Data CommunicationCommunications involving sensitive or secret data shall be done in a secure way to prevent eavesdropping, man in the middle attacks, replay vulnerabilities or that data in any way is altered.3 Anomalous Data TrafficAttacks associated with anomalous data traffic (e.g. DDoS, unreasonable values or patterns) shall be prevented by e.g. rate limiting, ingress and egress filters.4 Communication Channel EncryptionCommunication channels shall be protected by encryption. Industry standard encryption methods shall be supported. Multiple encryption methods may be used. Symmetric encryption shall be equal to AES128 or stronger. It must be able to change encryption method if the algorithm used is found vulnerable.4.4.7.5 General Cyber Security Requirements4.4.7.5.1 Cyber Security LevelsCyber Security LevelThe GRI/CEVT Cyber Security Team will conduct a threat analysis and risk assessment for all ECUs.Based on this judgment all ECUs are classified into four different security levels.Risk is assessed by combining the impact level and threat level together and classified as QM, low, medium, high and critical.Threat level parameters to estimate threat level include expertise, window of opportunity, equipment, and knowledge about TOE.Impact level parameters to estimate impact level include safety, financial, operational, privacy and legislation category.The four security levels are defined as: Cyber Security Level Components Description Level 1 - Low Non-algorithm relevant components, like common Sensors and Actuators Level 2 - Medium Vehicle Internal ECUs(including ECUs supporting UDS Diagnostics and/or software download) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Level 3 - High Key ECUs(typically domain masters or safety/privacy critical ECUs) Level 4 - Critical ECUs interacting with off board systems or otherwise highly exposed.(including connected ECUs communicating with off board systems directly) The security level for an ECU is given by the GRI/CEVT security team for each individual project.Complying to an assigned Cyber Security Level also implies fulfillment of all lower level requirements.E.g. a Level 3 Security Level ECU shall also comply to all Level 1 and 2 requirements.4.4.7.5.2 IntroductionMore and more vehicle systems are connected and at the same time there is an increasing cyber security threat. Even if a system is not directly exposed to an outside attacker the risk for indirect attacks via another compromised system cannot be neglected. To provide defense in depth and ensuring that the driver security, safety or privacy is not affected it is vital that all systems are designed with security in focus.These requirements shall be applied to all ECUs supporting UDS Diagnostics and/or software download4.5 Diagnostics4.5.1 Diagnostic and Bootloader Gateway Specification4.5.1.1 Gateway Generic4.5.1.1.1 General allocation of buffers requirements

title: Allocation of buffers from buffer pools
body: 1722 v3 Allocation of buffers from buffer pools Version history:(3):Purpose: To be able to specify max values for latency thru a gateway, there must also be a max time for allocating buffers.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 74649v2If the total size of messages does not exceed the total size of available memory for buffers, an in-vehicle gateway shall be able to allocate a suitable buffer for the message within 1ms.Rationale:Fragmentation of memory for buffers must be taken in account when implementing an Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU algorithm for allocation of buffers. Memory reserved for buffers should not be so fragmented so this time is exceeded, e.g. due to a need to run a de-fragmentation algorithm.Comment:Internal behaviour that is hard to measure from outside. Requirement should be verified with data/test result from supplier or inspection of implemented algorithm.

title: Static allocated buffers vs dynamic allocated buffers
body: 1723 v1 Static allocated buffers vs dynamic allocated buffers Version history:(1):Purpose: Indication to ECU supplier how much more memory that is needed if a static sized buffer algorithm is used instead of a dynamic sized buffer algorithmSource:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 436123v0If static sized buffers are used instead of dynamic sized buffers, it shall be estimated that at least 50% more memory is needed.Rationale:All buffer requirements assume a dynamic sized buffer algorithm, i.e. with efficient use of available memory without unused gaps in the memory.If using static sized message buffers and/or not possible to reserve separate buffers for request and responses: the project and the ECU supplier shall come to an agreement on used buffer structure to achieve similar performance, supplier shall count with that at least 50% more memory is needed when selecting hardware4.5.1.1.1 General allocation of buffers requirements, part 1This section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements:REQPROD 74649 Allocation of buffers from buffer poolsREQPROD 436123 Static allocated buffers vs dynamic allocated buffersThis document does not specify exactly how buffer allocation shall be implemented, this is up to the implementer. Allocation could e.g. be from dynamically sized message buffers or static sized message buffers in a buffer pool. However, the requirements on minimum RAM for buffers in the specification assume an efficient use of the available RAM, implicitly some sort of dynamic buffer allocation to be able to use most or the memory at all times. If a simpler static sized buffer allocation is used, the memory needs to be increased by at least 50% to achieve equal throughput as if a more complex and dynamic sized message buffer allocation is used.Since this a generic cross-platform specification, it cannot contain optimizations for all type of possible gateways.E.g. A gateway with only one network and one ECU connected does in practice not need same amount of memory as a gateway with two networks and 25 ECUs connected.Hence, optimization of buffer usage may be need to be handled by project and by gateway by gateway to get a compromise between efficiency and cost.There are also some rules that must be followed to get a predictable behavior with known maximum times for allocation. The time for allocating a buffer for a message must be within a Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU defined maximum time, i.e. buffer pool shall not be fragmented so that the time to allocate a buffer could increase to some unpredictable and unknown time.There must be some reserved buffers in buffer pools for a minimum number of request and response messages, to be able to receive messages from both directions request/downstream and response/upstream. I.e. all buffers cannot be allocated for requests/downstream, and vice versa not all buffers can be allocated for response/upstream so that one direction is starved out due to all buffers are allocated for the other direction.Below are two examples of two different buffer allocation algorithms: ![](images/9fb9c23dfc7dc9c7c9d6dbdf3b409d523916767895394f27e46f80c9ca05b5f3.jpg) Figure: Example buffer pool with dynamic sized message buffers Base Tech SWRS DHU 4.5.1.1.1.2 General allocation of buffers requirements, part 2 ![](images/c7fcc2b493f3963620136ea8e665c2c82dada19b88a4bf924e9f3f3c805732df.jpg) ## Figure: Example buffer pool with static sized message buffers ## 4.5.1.1.2 Parallel physical requests to different ECUs This section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements: · REQPROD 74200 Parallel physical requests to different ECUs · REQPROD 74201 Keep chronologic order of parallel requests · REQPROD 366460 Wait for available communication channel The external tester can send requests to different ECUs in parallel without waiting for response between the requests. Example: If external tester shall send two requests to two different targets, TA 0x211 and TAx311, external tester does not need to wait for response from first request to TA 0x211 before sending the next request to TA 0x311. The Backbone Network (FlexRay) supports multiple instances of transport protocol (TP) communication channels (CCs) to be able to send messages in parallel/simultaneously, see example in Figure " Overview three parallel request to three different target ECUs". GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Note-SWRS RELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No789(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU If the Vehicle GW can allocate a free communication channel on FlexRay, the next request can be sent to the Backbone Network (FlexRay) as soon as the next DoIP request is received. If no communication channel can be allocated, i.e. all communication channels occupied, the Vehicle GW must wait for next FlexRay cycle before re-trying to allocate a communication channel.The sequence of physical requests that is received in Vehicle GW from external tester shall be kept when Vehicle GW tries to allocate a communication channel.Example: Vehicle GW receives RequestA and RequestB, and requestA was received first but no communication channels are currently available. When a communication channel is available RequestA should be connected to this communication channel, and RequestB has to wait for next communication channel. Figure: Overview three parallel request to three different target ECUsSequence and more details regarding traffic on the networks for parallel requests, see section 'Parallel physical requests to different ECUs' and Figure "Sequence diagram three parallel GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No790(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU request to three different target ECUs".

title: Keep chronologic order of parallel physical messages
body: 1737 v4 Keep chronologic order of parallel physical messages Version history:(4):Purpose: Keep sequence of parallel physical requests.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74201v3The in-vehicle GW shall preserve the chronological order of received parallel physical request/responses when sending out the request/response on the networks.Rationale:Fair arbitration shall be implemented in the gateway, i.e. one channel may not starve another channel.Comment:A functional request as e.g. a tester present should have highest priority, and may be sent out before a physical request even if it arrives later to the gateway.

title: Parallel physical requests to different ECUs
body: 1738 v5 Parallel physical requests to different ECUs Version history:(5):Purpose: Speed up communication between tester and vehicle, by sending request to several networks and ECU in parallel/concurrent.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74200v4The in-vehicle GW shall support parallel requests to different ECUs (different target addresses).Rationale:Parallel request also leads to parallel responses from the target ECUs, including response pending and final response.Response pending and final response from a target ECU can come close an, i.e. without separation time between the two frames.Different target addresses includes the GW ECU, and if request is SWDL request the consequence is that GW ECU must be able to re-programming itself at the same time as requests are gatewayed to other ECUs.For example flashing of the GW ECU shall not disturb the gateway functionality to other ECUs.

title: Wait for available communication channel
body: 1739 v1 Wait for available communication channel Version history:(1): Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Purpose: Clarify that messages shall not be dropped if all communication channels are currently occupied. Message shall be kept and send as soon as a communication channel is releasedSource:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 366460v0If no communication channel can be allocated, i.e. all communication channels are currently occupied by other messages, the in-vehicle GW must wait until a communication channel is released and then send the message on the released communication channel.Rationale:No messages shall be dropped due to that there is currently no available communication channel.4.5.1.1.3 Functional requests to all ECUsThis section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements:REQPROD 74208 Functional requests transmit (Tx) CC(s)REQPROD 74213 Prioritize functional requestREQPROD 74215 Internal functional request handlingThe external tester can send the same request to all ECUs in the vehicle, see example in Figure " Overview functional request to all target ECUs". A variant of this could be to send functional request to all ECUs on a specific domain or network. See [GW_1] UDS Services for possible functional request addresses.Example: external tester sends a requests to all ECUs within the vehicle with TA 0xFFFF, to all ECUs on specific domain with 0xFF.Functional request should be unsegmented, hence it needs to be unsegmented on all types of networks, and this is specified in [GW_1] UDS Services.The in-vehicle gateway must be able to send a functional request to all connected network and the gateway ECU it self.An functional request, e.g. TesterPresent to keep the ECUs in a non-default session, shall always have a higher priority through the in-vehicle gateways over a physical request.The in-vehicle gateway should be able to open a separate transmit (Tx) communication channel (CC) for functional request for the respective network(s) connected to the gateway. I.e. separate CC(s) from the CCs for physical request so that a functional request (TesterPresent) is not jammed in the gateway.Note: the in-vehicle gateway does not check the data in the request, i.e. which service that are included in the functional request, hence this requirement will cover functional TesterPresent to keep ECUs in a non-default session ("keep alive logic").With a functional request with positive response suppressed (SPRMIB=TRUE), e.g. a functional TesterPresent for keeping a non-default session, there are (normally) not any Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU expected responses back from the ECUs. The in-vehicle gateways should also support functional request with positive response expected (SPRMIB=FALSE) and the in-vehicle gateways must be able to handle all responses from the ECUs. For the responses from a functional request (with many responses) the in-vehicle GWs must be able to send flow control WAIT if not all complete responses can be received directly due to out of buffers. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU The in-vehicle gateway shall be able to open separate transmit (Tx) communication channel(s) for functional request for the respective network(s) connected to the gateway.

title: Internal functional request handling
body: 1720 v3 Internal functional request handling Version history:(3):Purpose: A functional request could be to both the in-vehicle GW and the ECUs connected to the in-vehicle GW, i.e. the request should be received and executed by the in-vehicle GW and sent to other ECUs.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74215v2The in-vehicle GW shall be able route a functional request to all connected networks and to the in-vehicle GW it self.Comment:If the request will lead to a reset, the in-vehicle should first send out the request(s) on the network(s) before performing a reset of the in-vehicle GW, see requirement REQPROD 74087.

title: Prioritize functional request
body: 1721 v3 Prioritize functional request Version history:(3):Purpose: A functional TesterPresent must be able to reach a target ECU in non-default session, to keep the ECU in non-default session, independent of other possible physical request that could be queued in the gateway.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74213v2An in-vehicle gateway shall always prioritize a functional requests over a physical request.Rationale:An in-vehicle gateway does not check the content of a functional request, i.e. does not read the data field of the request, hence all functional request will include functional TesterPresent. 4.5.1.1.4 General In-vehicle gateway requirementsThis section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements:REQPROD 74072 Session layer time-out handlingREQPROD 74704 Transport layer routingREQPROD 74075 No re-sending of diagnostic requestsREQPROD 74077 No re-sending of diagnostic responsesREQPROD 74080 Release buffers on communication errorsREQPROD 74082 Flow control mechanism for diagnostic messagesREQPROD 74085 Separate CCs for request and responsesREQPROD 366516 Separate buffers for requests and responses Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU • REQPROD 74087 Transfer all functional request before a reset of gateway• REQPROD 74089 Gateway-on-the-fly• REQPROD 74168 Generic gateway latency requirement• REQPROD 74171 Routing table• REQPROD 366540 Multiple CPU design in the GW ECUThe diagnostic protocol between the tester and the vehicle is specified in [GW_12] DoIP and [GW_26] ISO DoIP ISO 13400-2.The in-vehicle gateways should be as simple and robust as possible, and e.g. leave complexity as re-sending a request to the tester (e.g. if no response from an ECU and tester times out).The in-vehicle gateways (Three types of gateways: Vehicle GW, Domain Network GW and Sub Network GW) should not do any validation or checks on responses from ECUs on Session layer level or above. The in-vehicle gateways should only work on transport protocol layer level and below, i.e. layer below where session layer timing parameters as e.g. P2, see [GW_3] UDS Session, is defined.An exception of this generic requirement may be needed for the Vehicle GW connected to the external tester, which may need to work in application level to e.g. differentiate if a response should be sent different external network as Ethernet, WLAN or CAN, or to an in-vehicle tester.The gateways in the vehicle shall have separate independent communication channels and buffers for downstream/request messages and upstream/response messages with flow control mechanisms where needed. The independent allocation of resources for request/downstream and response/upstream is important so that one direction does not starve out the other direction.see Figure "Gateway ECU handling network level".Channels on Transport layer level,with flowcontrol mechanismDownstream channel: From Tester to ECUUpstream channel: From ECU to Tester Figure: Gateway ECU handling network levelAn functional request, e.g. TesterPresent (see [GW_19] ISO 14229-1) to keep the ECUs in a non-default session, shall always have a higher priority through the in-vehicle gateways over a physical request.When dimension number communication channels and buffers in the in-vehicle gateways it should be guaranteed that messages are not lost during normal communication, e.g. during handling of parallel requests described later in this document.To be able to handle different speed and different size on frames on different networks, all Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU segmented messages should be routed through a transport layer.An in-vehicle gateway should never re-send messages if some error occurs, as. e.g. time-out errors (this is valid for both session layer time-outs and transport layer time-outs). One reason why the gateways in the vehicle should not do any re-sending is that the DP2, see [GW_3]UDS Session, would be unpredictable and a external tester would not know how long it should wait for response before a session layer time out.If a communication error occur, e.g. time-out in CAN network or connection lost on IP, the in-vehicle GWs should throw away the message(s) and release corresponding buffer(s).All possible errors from an ECU should be visible for the external tester, the gateways in the vehicle should not hide or correct responses from ECUs. The external tester should take the actions as e.g. re-send a message if needed.If a functional request is received that would lead to reset of the in-vehicle gateway, the in-vehicle gateway must send the functional request to all connected networks before the in-vehicle gateway to performs the reset, so that no functional requests are lost.A in-vehicle gateway can not guarantee that responses is not lost if the tester send a request that would lead to reset of the in-vehicle gateway. In the case when the tester expect a response, the tester should not send a request that would lead to reset of an in-vehicle gateway before the expected response is receive or a time-out on the expected response.To reduce latency, "gatewaying-on-the-fly" should where ever possible be used in the in-vehicle gateways. A diagnostic message should be sent as soon as possible, i.e. before a complete segmented message is received. If the network interface support this, e.g. Flexray and CAN, "gatewaying-on-the-fly" shall be used for these networks. A exception from this generic requirement is communication to and from the vehicle which will be message based due to the [GW_26] ISO DoIP protocol ISO 13400-2, i.e. only exception of this requirement if the network/standard does not support "gatewaying-on-the-fly".All in-vehicle gateway should have an routing table, describing the network topology behind the gateway.If a multiple CPU solution is used in the GW ECU for implementing the gateway functionality, the internal interface between the CPUs shall be design to still fulfil the GW ECU requirements.

title: Flow control mechanism for diagnostic messages
body: 1724 v3 Flow control mechanism for diagnostic messagesVersion history:(3):Purpose: Flow control mechanism needed for queued request, functional request functionality.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74082v2 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU An in-vehicle gateway shall support flow control mechanism on the connected networks, both for request/downstream and for responses/upstream.Rationale:No messages or frames shall be lost, if the receiver cannot receive the complete message directly due to out of “high level” buffers, it should be negotiated between sender and receiver when the remaining part can be sent. E.g. on FlexRay and CAN network using flow control frames WAIT and CTS. E.g. on IP network using TCP windows.

title: Gatewaying-on-the-fly
body: 1725 v4 Gatewaying-on-the-fly Version history:(4):Purpose: Reduce latency of forwarding diagnostic messages and possibility to save buffer memory (i.e. buffers less than the complete message can also be used to gateway messages)Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74089v3When both connected networks supports gatewaying-on-the-fly, the gateway shall use the gatewaying-on-the-fly functionality to reduce latency.Rationale:A diagnostic message should be sent as soon as possible, i.e. before a complete segmented message is received. If both network interface support this, e.g. Flexray and CAN, "gateway-on-the-fly" shall be used for these networks to reduce latency.Comment:The TP threshold for gatewaying-on-the-fly shall be used to for the complete transmission.Example if Flexray frame is 32 bytes, send data on Flexray when 26 bytes of data is available from CAN (the data part will be 26 bytes + 6 bytes "overhead" with e.g. address information in a Flexray CF frame).I.e. not only start to send the message when 26 bytes is received, and then continue with 7 bytes of data on Flexray when Flexray “catches” up on CAN.Fill the CF frames on Flexray with 26 bytes of data during the complete transmission, i.e. use as less overhead as possible in the Flexray frame.Comment:Communication between an external tester and the vehicle is an exception of this rule. This communication shall follow the DoIP protocol as specified in [GW_12] DoIP and [GW_26] ISO 13400-2.

title: Generic gateway latency requirement
body: 1726 v3 Generic gateway latency requirement Version history:(3):Purpose: Generic requirement for latency thru the gateway ECU. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74168v2When the gateway has received enough data on the receive (Rx) communication channel to fill an L-PDU on the transmit (Tx) side and the gateway can allocate a communication channel on the Tx side, start of transfer on the Tx side shall be within 10ms.Comment:For IP to IP communication the requirement is higher, 5ms, see [GW_14] InternetworksGeneral Specification REQPROD 40843

title: Multiple CPU design in the GW ECU
body: 1727 v2 Multiple CPU design in the GW ECU Version history:(2): Change the Verification Method to AnalysisPurpose:Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 366540v0If a multiple CPU solution is used in the GW ECU for implementing the gateway functionality, the internal interface between the CPUs shall be design to still fulfil the GW ECU requirements.Rationale:Latency requirement on the GW ECU shall be kept, which e.g implies that gateway-on-the-fly shall be used on the internal interface to keep the GW ECU latency requirement (e.g. 10ms requirement on GW ECU level).Any internal data transfer of a GW ECU shall never restrict the flow of gatewayed data, i.e. the internal data throughput must surpass the throughput of connected interfaces/networks by sufficient margin.If the IP ininterface is realized in one CPU and the Flexray interface is realized in an other CPU, the CPU on the IP side must be aware of current available resources in the CPU on the Flexray side regarding available communication channels and buffers. If the Flexray side runs out of resources for transmission of messages, the messages on the IP side must be halted until the resources on the Flexray side is released and available.No messages shall be dropped due to out of resources in one of the CPUs. Messages shall only be halted until resources are available and then continue with the transmission.

title: No re-sending of diagnostic requests
body: 1728 v3 No re-sending of diagnostic requests Version history:(3):Purpose: Keep internal gateways as simple as possible, and have a predictable in vehicle (delta)P2 time.Source:Verification Method: Test Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Legacy ID: 74075v2If a communication error occurs, an in-vehicle gateway shall not re-send a diagnostic request.Comment:Resending of diagnostic requests shall only be allowed for the external tester.

title: No re-sending of diagnostic responses
body: 1729 v3 No re-sending of diagnostic responses Version history:(3):Purpose: Keep internal target ECUs and gateway ECUs as simple as possible, and have a predictable in vehicle (delta)P2 time.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74077v2If a communication error occurs, an in-vehicle gateway shall not re-send a diagnostic response.

title: Release buffers on communication errors
body: 1730 v3 Release buffers on communication errors Version history:(3):Purpose: Not lock buffers, if a communication error occurs and the message cannot be sent or received. Requirement is on both sender and receiver side.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74080v2If a communication error occurs, the in-vehicle gateway shall release corresponding buffers used for the transmit (Tx) and/or receive (Rx) communication channels.

title: Routing table
body: 1731 v3 Routing table Version history:(3):Purpose: To be able to only route diagnostic messages which is supposed to be addressed to a specific Domain Network. For less complexity and maintenance is the diagnostic messages routed on network ID level.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74171v2An in-vehicle gateway shall have routing table for all possible paths to the ECUs after the gateway in the network topology, functionally addressed request included.Comment:See example in Figure "Example topology with routing tables". Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU

title: Separate buffers for requests and responses
body: 1732 v1 Separate buffers for requests and responses Version history:(1):Purpose: Request and response buffers must be independent of each other for supporting functionality as parallel requests and queued requestsSource:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 366516v0An in-vehicle gateway shall have separate and independent buffers for diagnostic request/downstream and for diagnostic responses/upstream.Rationale:All buffers can not be used for one way so that the other way is starved out and messages are dropped.

title: Separate CCs for request and responses
body: 1733 v3 Separate CCs for request and responses Version history:(3):Purpose: Request and response communication channels must be independent of each other for supporting functionality as parallel requests and queued requestsSource:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74085v2An in-vehicle gateway shall have separate and independent communication channels (CCs) for diagnostic request/downstream and for diagnostic responses/upstream.

title: Session layer time-out handling
body: 1734 v4 Session layer time-out handling Version history:(4):Purpose: Keep in-vehicle gateways as simple as possible. In-vehicle gateways shall not unpack and analyze data part of messages. Handling of Session layer time-outs, as e.g. P2 and P4, would require analysis of data and a higher level according to the OSI levels and more complex implementation.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74072v3An in-vehicle gateway shall not handle Session layer time-outs.Comment:Session layer time-outs handling (time-out between request and response message) shall only be handled by the external and/or internal tester. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU

title: Transfer all functional request before a reset of gateway
body: 1735 v3 Transfer all functional request before a reset of gateway Version history:(3):Purpose: Secure that no data is lost in the gateway due to reset of the gateway.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74087v2If an in-vehicle gateway receives a functional request that will lead to a reset of the in-vehicle gateway, the gateway shall first transmit all functional diagnostic to the connected network(s) before the gateway performs the reset.Comment:Implementation may differ depending on network type, e.g. CAN, FlexRay or IP network, depending on which functionality the network stack support, e.g. type of acknowledge that a message is sent.There is also requirements on the tester to avoid that messages are lost. The tester should not send a functional request that leads to reset with positive response expected (SPRMIB=FALSE), in this case there is a risk that the responses from the ECUs will be lost. A request to reset in-vehicle GW (functional or physical addressed) shall not be sent if there is pending request/responses in the vehicle. If the tester sends a request to reset a in-vehicle GW before all expected response from ECUs are received, there is a risk that responses are lost.

title: Transport layer routing
body: 1736 v3 Transport layer routing Version history:(3):Purpose: To be able to handle different speed and messaged sizes on different networksSource:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74704v2All segmented diagnostic messages shall be routed thru a transport layer with flow control mechanism.4.5.1.1.5 OverviewThis document describes and defines requirements for in-vehicle gateways for diagnostic communication for next generation of CEVT with the electrical architecture for the SPA platform.The interface for an external test tool to the vehicle for UDS diagnostic will be IP based using the DoIP standard in [GW_26] ISO 13400-2.This document does not specify any formal requirements for the physical communication link to the vehicle, it could e.g. be DoIP over Ethernet or DoIP over WLAN. The scope of the document is when a DoIP message is received in the vehicle, independent on used GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No801(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU communication link. Communication link to the vehicle is covered by other specification as e.g.[GW_12] DoIP, [GW_13] IP Routing Specification and [GW_14] Internetworks General Specification]. Figure: Overview external UDS tester connected to vehicleNote: A legislated OBD tester for CAN, e.g. scan tool, could be directly connected to CAN and is not included in the UDS view in Figure "Overview external UDS tester connected to vehicle".A J2534 test tool for CAN could also be connected to the vehicle through CAN (due to other legislated requirements), this traffic will pass the in-vehicle gateways. OBD tester should use 11 bit CAN ID and a J2534 tester should use 29 bit CAN ID. The vehicle GW will have a filter to receive for 29 bit CAN IDs for request from J2534, the 11 bit CAN IDs from a OBD test tool will not pass the vehicle GW. See section 'J2534 standard tester connected to Vehicle GW through CAN' for J2534 requirements. The ECU implements DoIP and is connected to external tester via IP and to the internal backbone network and IP network within the car. External Network Network for connection of an external tester. This saves memory and time. I.e. if MOST150 is used, diagnostic communication shall be IP based and sent on the 'Ethernet over MOST150' channel.Diagnostic communication over MOST25 is not covered in this version. If MOST25 should be used it would require e.g. diagnostic communication over MHP or similar protocol with flow control mechanism to be able to fulfill all requirements specified in this document.4.5.1.1.7Gateway description for DIAG and SWDLThis document describes and defines requirements for Diagnostic (DIAG) and Software download (SWDL) Gateway functionality in the vehicle.An example topology for diagnostic communication, UDS view, according to Figure "Example topology with routing tables, UDS view" is used as a base for other examples in this document.Note: The addresses used in to Figure "Example topology with routing tables, UDS view" is only example, allocation of addresses, e.g. CAN ID and IP addresses etc. will done in a project specific document for the project specific topology.Note: Legislated test tool for OBD diagnostic, e.g. scan tool, can be connected directly to CAN for the emission related ECU. This communication will not go trough gateways and are not included in the UDS view in Figure "Example topology with routing tables, UDS view".[GW_1]UDS Services specifies that an external tester shall have logical address 0x0E80 (in address range specified by [GW_26] ISO 13400-2). Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Figure: Example topology with routing tables, UDS viewNote: In the example in Figure "Example topology with routing tables, UDS view" ECU B and ECU H have same CAN ID for request and response. On 11 bit CAN normal addressing format the Domain ID information is lost.Both DIAG and SWDL use services specified in [GW_19] ISO 14229-1, however there are differences in which services in ISO 14229-1 that are used for DIAG and SWDL and how much data that are sent, see [GW_1] UDS Services and [GW_2] UDS Data.DIAG is executed in the application software, "application mode", hence resources as memory, CPU and networks capacity are limited and must be shared with other applications.SWDL is executed in the bootloader software, "program mode", where no other software is executed, hence SWDL has more memory, CPU and network capacity available than DIAG.For DIAG there are usually small requests from tester to vehicle, and greater responses from vehicle to tester. For SWDL the situation is normally reversed, large request from tester to vehicle, and small responses from vehicle to tester.On the Backbone Network (FlexRay) there will be two different schedules for application/DIAG GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document typeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No810(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU and bootloader/SWDL, see [GW_16] FlexRay Data Link Layer. This implies that the bandwidth for DIAG and SWDL on the Backbone Network (FlexRay) will differ.Due to these differences between SWDL and DIAG, requirements for e.g. allocation of number of buffers and buffers sizes will differ between SWDL and DIAG.The goal for this specification is that, where possible, have same requirements for DIAG and SWDL.For enhanced communication performance between tester and vehicle, the following features are supported in the in-vehicle gateways:For DIAG and SWDL:Parallel requests to different ECUsFunctional requests to all ECUsFor SWDL:Queued requests to same ECU4.5.1.1.7.1 Logical address formatThis sections does not describe any in-vehicle GW specific requirements, the section is included as an overview and information to better understand requirements in later sections.[GW_26] ISO 13400-2 specifies logical addresses that can be used by Vehicle manufacturers and CEVT will use the range:0x1000...0x7FFF Vehicle manufacturer specificHow the address range is used is specified in [GW_1] UDS Services.4.5.1.1.7.1.1 Logical address format for diagnostic request and responseThe addressing format for diagnostic request and response, source address(SA) and target address(TA), using Domain ID, Network ID and ECU ID is defined in [GW_1] UDS Services.See Figure "ECU address format for DIAG and SWDL" for an overview of the logical address format and how this is used in this document. Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU Figure: Sequence diagram two parallel request to two different target ECUs 4.5.1.3 Gateway Generic DIAG 4.5.1.3.1 Routing table This section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements: • REQPROD 77681 Protection of routing table • REQPROD 77682 Static routing rules • REQPROD 77683 Updateable routing table For application mode and diagnostic, it should be possible to update this routing table post build. The routing table for diagnostic messages should be static and not dependent on the content in the diagnostic message.

title: Protection of routing table
body: 1740 v3 Protection of routing table Version history: (3): Purpose: Protection of routing table of gateway when it is in use. Source: Verification Method: Analysis Legacy ID: 77681v2 Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU An in-vehicle gateway shall only allow reconfiguration of the routing table when the routing table is not in use (e.g. during programming mode).Rationale:Reconfiguration during normal operation (application running and routing table is in use) shall not be possible.Changes during normal operation are regarded as safety risk.

title: Static routing rules
body: 1741 v3 Static routing rules Version history:(3):Purpose: No dynamic routing, dependent on the content of a message.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 77682v2 An in-vehicle gateway shall only support statically defined routing rules.Rationale:The gateway shall not support dynamic routing rules for diagnostic messages. All routing paths shall be statically defined, and do not depend on the content of a diagnostic message.Reduction of complexity, realization of deterministic gateways.

title: Updateable routing table
body: 1742 v3 Updateable routing table Version history:(3):Purpose: Configuration routing table in gateway shall be updateable if a new ECU is added which is not included in the current routing table.Source:Verification Method: AnalysisLegacy ID: 77683v2 The routing configuration table in DIAG shall be updateable at post-build time.Rationale:The goal is to avoid re-compiling and re-loading of huge application binaries in case of minimal routing changes.Use case:A diagnostic request has to be routed to an additional path, e.g. a new ECU is added on a Domain network. Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU 4.5.1.4 Gateway Generic SWDL4.5.1.4.1 Gateway sequence diagramsThis section contain no new requirements, but describes in some more details example of traffic on the networks as consequence of the functionality described in section 'Queued physical requests to one ECU'4.5.1.4.1.1 Queued physical requests to same ECUThe functionality described in section 'Queued physical requests to one ECU' implies that flow control mechanism must be used, i.e. sending of flow control WAIT frames if next (queued) request not can be received yet, due to no available buffer.Figure: "Sequence diagram two queued request to one target ECU" gives an overview of the traffic on networks with flow control WAIT frames for queued requests. Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No816(1572) ![](images/ca77a3f8f0677bdcc89023a488651097fc461b7e4a3382133f1b845f91d6cbe3.jpg) Figure: Sequence diagram two queued request to one target ECU 4.5.1.4.2 Queued physical requests to one ECU This section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements: · REQPROD 74202 Queued physical requests to one ECU · REQPROD 74205 Keep chronological order for queued requests Messages to/from an external tester to/from an ECU in a topology as shown in Figure Example topology with routing tables, UDS view" may pass one or several gateways, depending on where in the topology the ECU is connected. Latency is introduced in each gateway step. GEELYGeely Automotive Research Institute(Ningbo)Co.Ltd Document TypeNote-SWRS Document Release StatusRELEASED Document No Revision005 Volume No01 Page No817(1572) Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Queued physical request is a feature to reduce the impact from this latency caused by the gateways (ΔP2, see [GW_3] UDS Session) for SWDL. Next request can be queued and already "loaded" in the vehicle and as soon the target ECU has processed the previous request, there is a new request ready in the queue. Next request can be received to the target ECU at the same time as the response from previous request is sent to the external tester. This implies that gateways and target ECU must have full duplex transport protocols for SWDL (or at least be able to send e.g. a flow control WAIT until the next request can be processed). Full duplex requirement is covered in other specifications for respective network.This implies that the external tester can send several requests to same ECUs for SWDL without waiting for response between the requests.Example: If an external tester shall send two requests to same target ECU, Request#1 and Request#2 to TA 0x211, the external tester does not need to wait for response from Request#1 before sending Request#2.The sequence of physical requests that is received in the vehicle from the external tester must be kept on all networks down to the target ECU. Same rule apply for the responses. Two queued messages in the vehicle should not use two different communication channels.On transport protocol layer level on the Domain Network, last frame of the first request must be sent before the first frame of the second request.Example: Request#1 is larger than Request#2, and if requests where sent in parallel in two independent communication channels on the FlexRay backbone, Request#2 may arrive before Request#1 in target ECU. This is not allowed! Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU Figure: Overview two queued request to one target ECU To be able to have a more predictable and not to long P2Client timer on the external tester side for the next/queued request, the external tester should not start the P2Client timer for the next/queued request when the DoIP ACK is received. When the response for the first request is received, or time out for the first request, then the external tester shall start the P2Client timer for the second request. Requirements regarding the P2Client timer can be found in [GW_3] UDS Session. Sequence and more details regarding traffic on the networks for queued requests, see section 'Queued physical requests to same ECU' and Figure "Sequence diagram two queued request to one target ECU".

title: Keep chronological order for queued messages
body: 1743 v4 Keep chronological order for queued messages Version history: (4): Purpose: If several queued diagnostic requests to one ECU, with same target address Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHUare sent thru the gateway, the chronological order of the request must be preserved.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74205v3The in-vehicle GW for SWDL shall preserve the chronological order of queued physical request/responses to/from a target ECU.Comment:Similar as REQPROD 74201 for parallel requests, but a queued request should not allocate a new available communication channel if the there is an ongoing transfer to same ECU.The queued (second) message shall never be sent out on a network before the first message.

title: Queued physical request to one ECU
body: 1744 v4 Queued physical request to one ECUVersion history:(4):Purpose: Speed up communication between tester and vehicle for SWDL, by reducing latency between requests to same ECU.Source:Verification Method: TestLegacy ID: 74202v3The in-vehicle GW for SWDL shall support at least one queued physical request to a target ECU (i.e. same target address in two requests).Rationale:Queued request also leads to queued responses from the target ECUs, including response pending and final response.Response pending and final response from a target ECU can come close an, i.e. without separation time between the two frames.Comment:Tester can send two requests to same target ECU without waiting for the response from the first request. The second request is called queued request.When tester receive the response from the first request, the tester can send next request, which now will be the queued request and so on.4.5.1.4.3 Routing tableThis section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements:• REQPROD 77685 Static routing configurationFor bootloader and software download it is not possible to update the routing table burned in to the non-volatile memory, so the routing table must be able to cover all possible connections from the start, so that a ECU can be added to the network topology with out updating the bootloader.

title: Static routing configuration

all possible ECU IDs in a network.This shall be implemented by either a range based approach or a table with defined spare addresses.Note:The table with defined spare addresses, if it exist for the project, are project specific and defined in 'Diagnostics and ECU platform' specification.Rationale:The goal is to avoid updating bootloader if ECUs are removed or added to a Domain network.Use case:A Document NameBase Tech SWRS DHU Comment:See example in Figure: "CAN diagnostic response frame structure".4.5.1.8 Vehicle Gateway - IP-CAN(Subnetwork)4.5.1.8.1 Gateway latency requirements4.5.1.8.1.1 IP - CAN diagnostic messages[VCC - DoCAN] specifies requirement on transport protocol level as e.g. maximum time between c consecutive frames, C_Cs, performance requirements.4.5.1.8.1.1.1 Diagnostic requests IP to CANThis section will describe and give grounds for the following requirements:REQPROD xxxxx Latency IP to CAN, GW_IP-CAN_L1The IP to CAN Vehicle GW shall receive and validate the complete request from IP before the request is transmitted on the Sub network (CAN), as specified in [ISO 13400-2]. See example in Figure: "Vehicle GW: IP to CAN request". Figure: Vehicle GW: IP to CAN requestDefinition of latency timing parameters:GW_IP-CAN_L1: Time between receiving the complete request from IP until first frame is sent out on Sub Network (CAN). Document Name Base Tech SWRS DHU GW_IP-CAN_L2: Time for transfer the complete request on Sub Network (CAN). This time depends on: • Size of the message, how the message is packed on the Sub Network (CAN), i.e. how many frames that shall be sent. • Timing parameters for the Sub Network (CAN) is specified in [VCC -DoCAN]. Flow control WAIT can only be sent a limited time, so GW_IP-CAN_L2 has impact on how the system shall be dimension regarding parallel communication channels and how many messages that can be received without sending Flow control WAIT frames.
